readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_a: Accuracy (with PPV, NPV, sensitivity, specificity) for conversion to AD within 36 months versus stable MCI, among ADNI MCI participants, single random 85/15 hold-out, tabular inputs (neuropsychological scores, FreeSurfer sMRI volumes and cortical thicknesses, CSF Abeta42/t-tau/p-tau, APOE e4).
readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_b: ROC AUC (and accuracy) for current-state MCI versus normal elderly controls, cross-sectional, 64 Shanghai community participants, leave-one-out cross-validation, inputs rs-fMRI and DTI connectivity edges.
grounds: Both PDFs are the papers the ledger IDs point to (the printed titles match the pack's PDF map and the corpus blocks for P-48 and P-56), so the mismatch lies in the record's claims, not in the PDFs.

Claim_b misreads P-56's dataset: its 64 participants were enrolled from the Shanghai Sanlin community, not ADNI.

readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_a: Binary accuracy and ROC AUC for MCI versus normal controls (also MCI versus SCD and SCD versus NC) from task-state prefrontal fNIRS connectivity plus cognitive-scale features, Chinese community and hospital sample, internal five-fold cross-validation.
readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_b: One-vs-rest ROC AUC for MCI (and macro-averaged per-class metrics) within a 3-class AD/MCI/normal classifier on T1 structural MRI, NACC-dominated multi-site sample, stratified internal five-fold cross-validation.
grounds: Both PDFs are the papers the ledger IDs point to (the printed titles match the pack's PDF map and the corpus blocks for P-85 and P-86), so the mismatch lies in the record's claims, not in the PDFs.
Claim_a misreads P-85's method: its models are nine classical classifiers run with default parameters on fNIRS connectivity and scale features, with no attention or self-attention component.
Claim_a misreads P-85's data: participants were recruited from hospitals and communities in Zhejiang and Shanghai, not taken from ADNI.
Claim_a's '88%' is not a P-85 result for any attention model; the paper's headline is MCI versus NC accuracy 92.0% and AUC 97.0% from classical models.

Claim_b misreads P-86's method: the CNN and GAT embeddings are concatenated and passed to a fully connected layer, with no SVM; the self-attention the record assigns to P-85 is in fact P-86's GAT branch.
Claim_b misreads P-86's data: 1,679 of its 1,900 scans (88%) come from NACC and only 145 (8%) from ADNI, so there is no 'same cohort' with P-85.
P-86 reports no 87% figure: its combined model's MCI AUC is 0.719 (72.3% in the Results text) in a 3-class AD/MCI/normal task.
The record describes no disagreement (a one-point gap it calls noise), and neither paper evaluates the other's method or claims the ordering the other would refute.
Independently of the misreadings, the pair fails the task, dataset-family and modality-family gates with no waiver, so a corrected record would be documented incommensurability, not genuine.

evidence_quotes.quote: Screening tools for subjective cognitive decline and mild cognitive impairment based on task-state prefrontal functional connectivity: a functional near-infrared spectroscopy study
A combined model of convolutional neural networks and graph attention networks for improved classification of mild cognitive impairment
Activated prefrontal FC data measured by fNIRS were collected from 55 normal controls, 80 SCD patients, and 111 MCI patients.
277 individuals were initially recruited including patients; caregivers; staff members and retirees of Kangci Hospital of Jiaxing and Shanghai Mental Health Center
based on the FC among the 10 ROIs under the time series for HBO, HBR and HBT signals along with the scores and completion times for the MMSE, BNT and HVLT
we employed nine widely used machine learning models, including LDA, LR, GNB, SVM, KNN, RF, XGBoost, GBDT, and RUSboost
All parameters used in the nine models were consistent with those suggested by default in Classifier of Python 3.11.
Five-fold cross-validation was adopted to divide the samples into four training sets and one test set

record_defects: claim_a: P-85 contains no attention-based or self-attention fusion; it feeds PCA-reduced fNIRS connectivity and cognitive-scale features to nine classical classifiers with default parameters.
claim_a: P-85 is not an ADNI study; its 246 participants were recruited in Zhejiang and Shanghai.

claim_a: '88%' is not a P-85 result for the stated method; the paper's headline is MCI versus NC accuracy 0.920 and AUC 0.970, and its accuracies near 87-89% are classical-model results (e.g. SVM 0.884 in the HVLT task).
claim_b: P-86 uses no SVM; the CNN and GAT embeddings are concatenated and passed to a fully connected layer.
claim_b: P-86 is not 'ADNI with same cohort': 1,679 of its 1,900 scans are NACC, 145 ADNI and 76 Hanyang, and it shares no participants with P-85.
claim_b: P-86 reports no 87% figure; its combined model's MCI AUC is 0.719 (72.3% in the Results text) and its AD AUC 86.5%.
The claims appear transposed: the attention mechanism belongs to P-86 (GAT self-attention) and the SVM to P-85 (one of its nine classifiers), and neither paper matches the claim filed against it.
task_equivalence true: P-85 runs NC/SCD/MCI binary tasks and P-86 a 3-class AD/MCI/normal task.
dataset_family_equivalence true: the samples come from different sources (P-85's own Chinese recruits versus NACC-dominated multi-site data).
apparent_performance_gap '1 percentage point (88% vs 87%)': neither figure is reported for the designs named, so the gap is an artefact of the claims.
resolution_note 'both fusion->SVM pathway': P-86 has no SVM, and 'attention regularisation' has no referent in P-85; the stored text also carries a mis-encoded arrow ('fusionâ†’SVM').
modality_family 'digital_behaviour|structural_mri': P-85's modality is fNIRS with paper-and-pencil scales, not digital behaviour (the 'No' equality outcome is nonetheless correct).

record_defects: claim_b 'Structural MRI outperforms NP scores (79% vs 72%)': P-96 has no MRI data and no NP-test predictors, and prints no 79% or 72%; its model is a seven-variable physical-examination/blood-test random forest (accuracy 85.5%, AUROC 0.93).

claim_a '(83% vs 76%)': no such NP-vs-NR pair is printed in P-95's text or tables. The NR groups are mostly below 50% accuracy, and Table 7 has no NR rows (the 83.4 and 76.5 in it are NP-group AUROCs for LR/NB and C4.5). P-95's best NP combination is 79.78% accuracy (SVM) and its all-feature best is 81.00% (naive Bayes). Its NR set is DTI, visual rating scales and subcortical volumes, not structural MRI alone.
apparent_performance_gap 'MRI > NP in P-96' is false; P-96 makes no modality ranking.
resolution_note 'P-95 uses CHARLS cognitive cohort' is false: P-95 is a Novi Sad (Serbia) clinical cohort. CHARLS is P-96's cohort.
resolution_note 'P-96 uses ADNI' is false: P-96 uses CHARLS 2015, Yiwu 2021 and CHARLS 2011, and ADNI is not mentioned in the paper.

resolution_note 'NP test batteries differ (MMSE + vocabulary vs MMSE + CDR + HVLT)' is false for both papers. P-95's NP set is MMSE, ACE III, RAVLT, ROCF, TMT, WMS-R, WAIS (similarities, cube, code), BNT, fluency, EXIT25, FAB, WCST and HVO, plus depression, NPI, quality-of-life and daily-living scales, with no CDR, HVLT or vocabulary test. P-96 has no NP battery among its predictors; the MMSE only defines its outcome.
task_equivalence=true is false: 3-class clinical diagnosis vs binary screening for an MMSE-defined label.
modality_family 'clinical_survey' with modality_family_equal 'Yes' is false: NP tests against MRI-derived features in P-95; physical examination and blood tests in P-96.
The rejection reason ('dataset-specific battery composition explains ranking conflict') presupposes a ranking conflict that neither PDF contains.

readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_a: Classification accuracy for binary MCI vs NC from DTI + rs-fMRI connectome fusion, ADNI 214 subjects, 5-fold CV. The headline 92.7% is the Best column of the best setting; that setting's average is 86.3%.
readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_b: Mean accuracy and quadratic weighted kappa over 100 repeats of 5-fold CV for 4-class HC/EMCI/LMCI/AD staging from rs-fMRI-only functional-connectivity embeddings, ADNI 125 subjects.
grounds: Claim_a misreads P-92. P-92 reports accuracy, not AUC; its headline is 92.7% (the Best column for the best setting, average 86.3%) for binary MCI vs NC, and no 91% AUC appears. Only the dropout detail is correct (ratio 0.6).

Claim_b misreads P-97. P-97 uses rs-fMRI only (no DTI) and concatenates node2vec node embeddings from a single functional graph rather than DTI and fMRI features. It reports accuracy and quadratic kappa, not AUC (97.73% for a 4-class task), on its own 125-subject sample, not 'the same validation set' as P-92.
The record itself describes no disagreement: its resolution note calls the gap expected and 'marginal not fundamental', which is a spread between two methods rather than a contradiction.

Read against the documents, the pair holds no incompatible claim either: the tasks differ (binary vs 4-class), as do the modality sets (DTI + fMRI vs fMRI) and the accuracy summaries (Best column vs repeated-CV mean). P-97 also meets the performance-validity exclusion, so the pair could not be genuine even if re-drafted.

record_defects: claim_a '91% AUC': P-92 reports no AUC in its text, tables or figure captions. Its headline is accuracy, 92.7% (Best column of the best setting; average 86.3%), and on the second ADNI subset 94.1% (average 92.0%). The dropout detail is correct (ratio 0.6).

claim_b 'DTI + rs-fMRI simple concatenation': P-97 uses no DTI (rs-fMRI only, with T1 in preprocessing). Its concatenation is of node2vec node embeddings from one functional graph, not multimodal feature concatenation.
claim_b '89% AUC': P-97 reports no AUC. It gives accuracy 97.73% (SVM) / 97.32% (LR) with its mapping function and 87.2% / 86.96% without, and quadratic kappa 96.86% / 96.74%.
claim_b 'on same validation set' is false: P-97 used its own 125-subject ADNI sample with four classes; P-92 used 214 (and 124) subjects with two classes.
task_equivalence=true is false: binary MCI vs NC against 4-class HC/EMCI/LMCI/AD.
modality_family 'functional_mri' with modality_family_equal 'Yes' overstates the match: P-92 is a DTI + rs-fMRI fusion, P-97 is rs-fMRI only.
apparent_performance_gap '2 percentage points (91% vs 89%)': neither figure is in either paper, and the headline accuracies the papers do print (92.7% binary; 97.73% 4-class) are not comparable.

resolution_note 'both approaches are variants of DTI+fMRI fusion' and 'Graph representation > concatenation' are false: P-97 is not a fusion method, and it is itself a graph-embedding method (node2vec random walks on a functional connectivity graph).

Provenance: the record's claims and note are unchanged since its first commit (087db63, 2026-03-28). At that commit the summary blocks already gave P-92 as 92.7% accuracy for MCI vs NC and P-97 as 97.73% accuracy / 96.86% kappa for 4-class staging, so the 91%/89% AUC figures were not taken from the blocks.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: Two CHARLS random-forest models for AACD-defined MCI disagree: P-27 (older adults with depressive symptoms, self-report predictors) reported AUC 0.826 in training (0.801 internal, 0.653 external), against 0.93 in P-96's training set (0.83 and 0.87 external), whose predictors are education, grip strength, anthropometry and routine blood values (z = 7.8 on the training figures, over 12 on the external ones). The depression-restricted sample, the predictor sets, the label instrument and P-96's apparently class-balanced evaluation sets are candidate explanations, none shown to be sufficient.
candidate_explanations: P-27 restricts its population to older adults with depressive symptoms (CESD-10 >= 10).
The predictor sets differ: self-report variables (P-27) against education plus grip strength, anthropometry and routine blood values (P-96).
The label instruments differ: the HRS-style CHARLS battery (P-27) against a score P-96 calls the MMSE, both under an AACD definition.
The external cohorts differ: CLHLS scored with the CMMSE (P-27) against Yiwu 2021 and CHARLS 2011 (P-96).

P-96's Table 3 PPV and accuracy, its AUPRC and its external AUROC intervals all imply class-balanced (resampled) evaluation sets, although its text denies that SMOTE was applied to test or external sets. Its AUROCs may therefore be optimistic, but this is not shown to close the gap.
P-27's 0.826 is an apparent training AUC after SMOTE; its internal figure is 0.801 and its CV figure 0.791.
The CHARLS waves overlap, so the samples are not independent.
None is shown to be sufficient.

None is shown to be sufficient.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For MCI versus controls from structural MRI, a hippocampal-radiomics XGBoost model reported test AUC 0.864 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.89) on a single 45-subject split (P-52), against 0.735 by 10-fold CV in 207 participants (P-99). The difference is marginal: z = 2.40 on the printed interval and 2.02 with a sample-size SE, but below 1.96 on other readings of P-52's asymmetric interval. P-52's tabulated control MoCA (22.5) also contradicts its stated control criterion (MoCA 27 or above).
candidate_explanations: P-52's control label: it states MoCA >= 27, but the tabulated NC MoCA is 22.3-22.7 in every column, below its own impairment cut-off, and MCI and NC do not differ on MoCA (p = 0.17) or MMSE (p = 0.09).
P-52 z-scored features against the entire cohort, and its hypothesis-test filter is not stated to be training-only, so information may have leaked into the test set.
P-52 relies on a single 45-subject split; P-99 uses 10-fold CV on 207 participants.
The features differ: hippocampal radiomics against whole-brain FreeSurfer morphometry.
The classifiers differ: XGBoost against SVC. P-99's own XGBoost scored 0.644.
The MCI labels differ: cut-off based (P-52) against an ICD-10 F06.7 memory-clinic diagnosis (P-99).
P-99's best-of-six model selection and its age imbalance both run against the observed gap.
The scanners differ: 1.5T Toshiba (P-99), with P-52's protocol only in its supplement.
None is shown to be sufficient.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For pMCI vs sMCI from structural MRI in ADNI, P-122's model on two scans per subject reports 84.28% accuracy (AUC 0.860; six-fold CV, 275 subjects), against 74.61% (AUC 0.780; 5-fold CV, 593 subjects) for P-3's single-baseline-scan model. The gap is beyond combined uncertainty (z = 3.42 for accuracy, 2.64 for AUC), and neither paper reconciles it. Candidate explanations are longitudinal against single-scan input, sample-level scoring, 2D slices and label definition, and neither paper shows any of them to be sufficient.
candidate_explanations: Two-timepoint longitudinal input (P-122) against a single baseline scan (P-3). P-122 does not state the interval between the scans, or whether the later scan comes before conversion.
Unit of analysis: accuracy over longitudinal samples (about three per subject) against one prediction per subject.
Input representation: 2D axial slice sequences against whole 3D volumes.
Label definition and cohort: DSM-5-guided selection from ADNI 1/GO/2/3 with no stated window, against dementia within 36 months in ADNI1/2.
Data augmentation in P-122.
P-3 tunes and selects its models on the evaluation folds, which biases P-3 upward, against the gap.
Neither paper shows any of these to be sufficient.
unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.review_status: adopted on the operator's decision of 2026-09-30

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For predicting progression from MCI to AD or dementia in ADNI from cognitive and MRI data, P-168 reports AUC 0.90 from a single-timepoint model (0.93 with five visits; 10-fold CV, 347 participants, 2-year horizon), and P-156 reports AUC 0.81 from baseline data on a 169-patient held-out set. The matched figures differ only just beyond combined uncertainty (z = 2.01), a margin that depends on P-156's unprinted test class split. Horizon, cohort selection, index timepoint and validation design are candidate explanations, none shown to be sufficient.
candidate_explanations: Horizon: fixed 2 years from a month-24 index exam (P-168) vs latest recorded diagnosis (P-156). P-156 p4: 'The most recent diagnosis given to each patient (Final DX) was the outcome predicted'.
Cohort construction: P-168 is complete-case, five visits, still MCI at month 24, and excludes 187 with undetermined status at month 48; P-156 takes all 841 baseline EMCI/LMCI.
Index timepoint: P-168's single-timepoint model uses the month-24 exam, not the first MCI visit. The longitudinal effect it quantifies (0.03, DeLong P = 0.039) explains only part of the gap.
Validation optimism in P-168: hyperparameters were tuned by 10-fold CV on the same 347 participants that were later scored by 10-fold CV.
Validation design: 10-fold CV mean (P-168) vs a single random 20% held-out test set (P-156).
Feature loss and processing in P-156: PET and DTI were dropped for missingness, and TADPOLE merges ADNI editions.
Label and case mix: AD vs dementia; 35.4% of P-156's cohort is early MCI.
None of these is shown to be sufficient.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: P-178 reports AUC 0.96 (accuracy 93.6%) for predicting conversion of ADNI early MCI to AD from cognitive scores, APOE4, demographics and two MRI volumes. P-185 reports AUC 0.6951 (accuracy 69.37%) for 3-year conversion in ADNI-1 MCI from MRI morphometry alone. The gap exceeds combined uncertainty (z = 4.99) and neither paper explains it; the candidate explanations are the non-shared cognitive predictors, the open horizon and early-MCI population, and P-178's visit-level oversampled single-split evaluation.
candidate_explanations: Predictor set: P-178 adds ADAS13, ADAS11, FAQ, MMSE, age, race and APOE4 to two MRI volumes; P-185 uses MRI only. P-178's 6-feature model without MRI or APOE4 still reaches AUC 0.88, but P-178 has no MRI-only model.
Label and horizon: last-visit diagnosis (open horizon) against conversion within 3 years.
Population and prevalence: ADNI-GO/2 early MCI with 49/383 converters against ADNI-1 MCI with 126/221.

Unit of analysis and evaluation (P-178): oversampled visit records from one random split. Table 1 (balanced 402/402 test set) contradicts Table 4, which implies an imbalanced test set with about 56% of converter visits identified.
Model selection on test accuracy (P-178): the nine-feature group was chosen because 'our accuracy rose to 93.6%'.
Neither paper shows any of these to be sufficient.
unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.review_status: adopted on the operator's decision of 2026-09-30

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For progressive versus stable MCI from structural MRI in ADNI, a hippocampal-box DenseNet trained on AD versus controls reached 75.85% accuracy (AUC 0.777) on 381 subjects (P-182), and a two-timepoint whole-brain CNN-Transformer reached 84.28% in six-fold CV over 275 subjects (AUC 0.860; headline 84.74%) (P-122). The gap is beyond combined uncertainty (z = 2.72) and unexplained, and its candidate explanations have not been tested.
candidate_explanations: Architecture: P-122's multi-scale attention and fusion modules. Its own ablation (unimproved Eff-GCNet 71.6%, AUC 0.7770) uses P-122's own input, label and target, not P-182's condition, so it is not shown to be sufficient for the gap between the papers.
Input: two time points (P-122) vs one baseline scan (P-182: 'we did not examine longitudinal changes in imaging metrics').
Input region: P-182 uses only a 3D box around the hippocampus.
Training target: P-182 trains on AD vs CN and transfers to MCI.

Label window: P-182 requires evaluations at least 18 months apart and excludes 65 reverters. P-122 gives no window beyond 'guided by DSM-5 criteria', and it does not say whether the later scan precedes conversion.
Unit of analysis and validation: P-122 scores samples and aggregates both validation schemes. Its ablation tables fit a 102-case test set (42/60), not the stated 124.
Single modality, which P-182 names as possibly lowering its performance.
None is shown by either paper to be sufficient.
unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.review_status: adopted on the operator's decision of 2026-09-30

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For predicting conversion from MCI in ADNI from cognitive and MRI measures, a longitudinal forecast model reached AUC 0.957 one year ahead (5-fold CV, n = 85) (P-186), and a baseline-only multimodal ensemble reached AUC 0.81 on 169 held-out patients (P-156). The difference is beyond combined uncertainty (z = 3.26) and unexplained, and the candidate explanations are not shown to be sufficient.
candidate_explanations: Input anchored to the conversion time: P-186 uses a forecast value, while P-156 uses baseline only. P-186 prints no baseline-only comparator.
Outcome window: before month 36 (P-186) vs the most recent diagnosis with no fixed horizon (P-156).
P-186 optimism: scaling before the split, t-test ranking on the full n=85 dataset (Figure 1), and reporting of the best marker-set size.
Cohort subset: an ADNI-1 completers subsample (n=85) vs 841 TADPOLE MCI patients.
P-156 feature set: modalities with 30% or more missing values dropped (PET, DTI), KNN imputation, and CSF/demographics/APOE added.
Validation: a 5-fold CV average vs one 80/20 split.
None is shown to be sufficient.
unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.review_status: adopted on the operator's decision of 2026-09-30

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For three-year MCI-to-AD conversion from baseline structural MRI in ADNI, coupled grey-matter network features reached 87.72% accuracy (10-fold CV, n = 234) (P-207) against 69.37% for AD/NC-subspace cortical features (20x10-fold CV, n = 221) (P-185). The difference is beyond combined uncertainty (z = 4.87) and unexplained. Candidate explanations not shown to be sufficient are the feature representation, P-207's parameter setting (its median setting gives 75.71%) and its transductive coupling.
candidate_explanations: Feature representation: ICA-network coupled GMV (P-207) vs FreeSurfer CT/CV projected into an AD/NC subspace (P-185). Neither paper evaluates the other's representation.
Parameter setting: P-207's E1=3/E2=2 was carried over from AD vs NC and is also the maximum of the 15 MCI settings (median 75.71%, which gives z = 1.52). P-185 also tuned its parameters.
Transductive unsupervised coupling: P-207 computes Pearson/CCA weights over all subjects of the task, with no within-fold estimation described.
Classifier: AdaBoost of linear SVMs vs a single linear SVM.
Scanners and subjects: mixed 1.5T/3T with 108 MCI-nc vs 1.5T only with 95 sMCI.
Validation: a single 10-fold CV vs 20 repeats of 10-fold CV.
None is shown to be sufficient.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: At the matched three-year horizon, the MRI-based model of Cai et al. (P-211; regional MRI measures with demographics and APOE4, no cognitive tests) reached a cross-validated AUC of about 0.70 (read from its Figure 2d), below the AUC of 0.827 that Bae et al. (P-37) report for a 3D CNN on baseline T1 scans (z = 2.2, a narrow margin), which reverses the recorded comparison (0.92 vs 0.827, which set P-211's five-year figure against a three-year one and cited the P-174 duplicate stub).
candidate_explanations: Label definition: P-37 keeps later converters and short-follow-up MCI out of the stable group ('MCI subjects with a duration of MCI less than 3 years without conversion were excluded due to the potential possibility of near-future conversion.'). P-211's 3-year negatives include later converters, and P-211 attributes its 3-year dip to them ('these false positives represent individuals whose diagnostic classification did not change during the short-term follow-up period, despite the disease progressing and eventually reaching the dementia stage at a later time point'). It prints no 3-year AUC with them removed.
Input representation and model: ten FreeSurfer regional measures plus covariates in an EBM (P-211) against a transfer-learned 3D CNN on the whole T1 image (P-37).
Pretraining (P-37): 'The source task used 1406 DAT and 2084 NC scans from 1080 subjects.' P-211 trains on MCI only.
Validation design: one random 68-scan held-out test (P-37) against 5-fold CV with SMOTE (P-211: 'All EBMs were tested with the 5-fold cross validation.').
Index scan and cohort: P-37 uses 'the single time point sMRI scan at which an individual first received a diagnosis of MCI'; P-211 uses the ADNI baseline visit of amnestic MCI from ADNI1/2/3/GO.
None of these is shown by either paper to be sufficient.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For three-year MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI, Liu et al. (P-93) report AUC 0.838 on an independent MRI-only test set, while the MRI model without cognitive scores of Cai et al. (P-211) reaches about 0.70 in cross-validation (read from its Figure 2d; z = 3.4), the reverse of the recorded 0.92 vs 0.838, which set P-211's five-year multimodal figure against a 36-month one.
candidate_explanations: Input representation and model: a deep network on whole-brain T1 with GAN-synthesised PET features (P-93) against an EBM on tabular FreeSurfer measures ('Comb. (c) MRI-driven biomarkers, plus age, gender, education, diagnose at baseline, and APOE4.').
Training data (P-93): 'That is, sMCI and sCN are treated as the negative category, pMCI and AD are used as the positive category.' (939 subjects with real PET).
Validation design (P-211): SMOTE, a 90/10 split and 5-fold CV; its single 3-year test figure (0.81) sits above its plotted CV means.
Test-set composition (P-93): 96 pMCI/81 sMCI in the text against 93/66 in Tables 2 and 5.
Label construction near the horizon (P-211): later converters counted as negatives cause its 3-year dip, but P-93 uses the same 36-month window, so this is not shown to separate the papers.
None of these is shown by either paper to be sufficient.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI, Guan et al. (P-229) report AUC 0.757 from grey-matter volumes alone, with a classifier trained only on AD/NC labels, against AUC 0.96 for the random forest of Velazquez and Lee (P-178), which combines two MRI volumes with cognitive scores, APOE4 and demographics in early MCI over an open horizon (z = 4.3). P-178's figure is visit-level, its feature set was chosen on its test split, and its tables disagree on the test-set size.
candidate_explanations: Predictor set: P-178 adds ADAS13, ADAS11, FAQ, MMSE, APOE4, age and race to two MRI volumes; its model without MRI and APOE4 still has AUC 0.88, but that is not an MRI-only comparison.
Horizon and label: conversion by the last visit (mean 5.02 years) in P-178 against within 36 months in P-229.
Training design (P-229): the MCI subjects are an unlabelled target domain, with AD/NC as the labelled source.
Population: early MCI only (P-178) against unselected ADNI MCI (P-229).
Unit of analysis and reporting (P-178): visit-level training and testing; the Table 1 test count (402/402) contradicts Table 4.
Model selection on the test split (P-178): 'by removing the RAVLT features, our accuracy rose to 93.6%'.
None of these is shown by either paper to be sufficient.
unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.review_status: adopted on the operator's decision of 2026-09-30

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For three-year MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI from structural-MRI grey-matter volumes, Liu et al. (P-207) report 87.72% accuracy (10-fold CV, 234 MCI) with a coupled network representation, against 73.54% for Guan et al. (P-229) on 393 MCI with a classifier trained only on AD/NC labels (z = 4.6). The two papers' plain regional-volume baselines coincide (64.15% and 64.12%), which points to the methods, but neither paper reports a figure under the other's conditions.
candidate_explanations: Feature representation (P-207): 'The best classification accuracies for different features are 64.15% for OFMROI, 75.10% for CFMROI, 68.62% for OFMnetwork, and 87.72% for CFMnetwork.'
Training design: P-229's classifier never sees MCI labels (AD/NC source, unlabelled MCI target); P-207 trains on MCI labels by 10-fold CV.
Parameter selection (P-207): E1 and E2 searched over {2,3,4} x {1..5}; the AD/NC-chosen setting is also the MCI maximum, and the other settings give 70.24-82.31%.
Label definition: P-207's MCI-nc are 'otherwise', with no minimum follow-up stated, against P-229's 36-month stable group.
Region set and sample: the top 3 ROIs per AD/NC-derived ICA network on 234 MCI (P-207) against 90 AAL regions on 393 MCI (P-229).
Coupling weights (P-207) are computed across subjects, and the paper does not say this was done inside the training folds.
None of these is shown by either paper to be sufficient for the cross-paper gap.
unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.review_status: adopted on the operator's decision of 2026-09-30

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: On MRI alone, in ADNI MCI with 5-fold cross-validation, P-239's radiomics branch predicts time to AD conversion with a C-index of 0.67 against 0.756 for P-241's S-CNN (z = 2.5; P-241's other MRI models give 0.73-0.75, two within uncertainty of 0.67). That is the reverse of the recorded 0.85 versus 0.676, which set P-239's clinical-plus-MRI model against P-241's external NACC result.
candidate_explanations: Features within the MRI channel: P-239 CSF texture radiomics 'the optimal combination of [CSF][texture] features was utilized as the radiomics input for our proposed model' vs P-241 raw T1 (S-CNN) or grey-matter volumes.
P-239 states its radiomics input is weak: 'radiomics features may contribute less to the multi-model and may potentially introduce bias into the overall network' (statement, not demonstration).
C-index computation: P-241 'Concordance indices were averaged over the 3 time bins (24 months, 48 months, 108 months) for each fold.'
Population: P-239 excludes reverters and pools eMCI (92% censored) with lMCI (55.3%); P-241 counts reverters as 'non-converters'.
P-239 time-to-event construction: 'the conversion time is calculated by adding the delaying time to their most recent visits.'
P-241's ADNI discovery set is the one divided by CSF amyloid quartiles, suggesting a CSF-available subset (inclusion rules not in the held text).
None is shown by either paper to be sufficient.
unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.review_status: adopted on the operator's decision of 2026-09-30

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI, P-244 reports time-dependent AUCs of 0.957 at 5 years and 0.914 at 3 years, against P-198's 0.78 for conversion within about 2 years. P-244's own 1-year AUC (0.810) agrees with P-198, so the gap may be partly a horizon effect as well as P-244's added cognitive predictors, and neither paper reports a result at the other's horizon.
candidate_explanations: Predictor set: P-244 'concatenated the baseline clinical features and neuroimaging features extracted from the MRI scans'; P-198 uses five cortical-thickness covariates only. P-244 has no MRI-only arm.
Horizon: P-198 predicts transition 'within the next two years'; P-244's AUC rises with horizon, and its 1-year 0.810 agrees with P-198.

Possible internal optimism in P-244: internal MMSE AUCs are 0.537-0.600, but in AIBL (30 MCI) the Deep-AD C-index is 0.752 against MMSE's 0.730, and the external AUCs are described only as 'consistently comparative performance with MMSE'.
Time conditioning in P-244 training (q(z|x,t)); the paper says inference uses 'data x at the starting point' only.
P-198's Relief top-five feature selection is not stated to be nested in the folds. This would inflate 0.78, so it would widen the gap rather than close it.
Inclusion and follow-up: P-244 requires at least two MRI scans and follows up to 10 years with censoring; P-198 requires a follow-up scan about 2 years after baseline.
P-244's SEs rest on assumed per-horizon counts.
None is shown by either paper to be sufficient.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: Among older drivers, P-69's naturalistic-driving model separates cognitively impaired from healthy drivers with 96% accuracy (balanced 0.87, on 15 impaired and 90 healthy test drivers). P-331 reaches 67-69% (balanced 0.64-0.67) on the same demographics-plus-driving inputs. The gap survives the class-mix difference but rests on P-69's I-score-selected models: its other classifiers on the same inputs are within uncertainty of P-331.
candidate_explanations: Class mix and operating point: 14% vs 61% impaired; P-331 selects models by F1 ('optimizing the balance between precision and recall'); P-69 tests on 90 healthy and 15 impaired drivers.

I-score selection carries the gap. Without it, P-69's RF (BA 0.700, z 0.74), ResBlocks (0.767, z 1.58) and logistic regression (0.778, z 1.75) on the same inputs are within uncertainty of P-331. The modules come from 'Applying BDA to the dementia dataset', with no stated hold-out of the test cases.
Demographic and site signal: P-69's top module includes 'Age ... Region (study site)', and its ResBlocks on demographics alone reach BA 0.839.
Label timing: P-69 uses the most severe diagnosis during follow-up among drivers intact at enrolment; P-331 uses baseline status. P-331's one-year-ahead model (BA 0.694) still gives z 2.37.
Label source: annual-interview labels (P-69) vs assessment by two dementia-specialist clinicians under NIA-AA (P-331).
Case mix: 36 MCI / 25 dementia (P-69) vs 64 MCI / 8 dementia (P-331).
Monitoring length and features: 10-44 months with 48 time-series features per variable (P-69) vs three months of weekly aggregates (P-331).
Validation: one random split with 15 impaired test cases and SMOTE (P-69) vs nested LOSO-CV with majority voting (P-331).
None is shown by either paper to be sufficient.
unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.review_status: adopted on the operator's decision of 2026-09-30

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For MCI-to-AD progression in ADNI, P-244's clinical-plus-MRI survival model reports a 3-year time-dependent AUC of 0.914, against 0.74 for P-356's hippocampal-slice vision transformer at 36 months (z = 2.9). Candidate explanations, none shown to be sufficient, are P-244's added cognitive and APOE4 predictors, its survival estimand and its unprinted external AUCs.
candidate_explanations: Predictor set: P-244 adds cognitive/clinical scores and APOE4 to FreeSurfer morphometry; P-356 'solely focused on MRI features'. P-244 has no MRI-only model.
Estimand and censoring: time-dependent AUC over all MCI with 55.56% right censored (P-244) vs a cleaned dichotomy (P-356). The cleaning favours P-356, so it does not explain P-356's lower figure.
Label cleaning in P-356: stable MCI must hold its status for at least three years and at all follow-ups; reverters are excluded.
Possible internal optimism in P-244: the external AIBL C-index is 0.752 against MMSE's 0.730, and the external AUCs are described only as 'consistently comparative performance with MMSE'.
Time conditioning in P-244 training; the paper says inference uses baseline x only.
Validation and inclusion: 5-fold CV among participants with at least two MRI scans (P-244) vs one 70/15/15 split with about 86 test subjects (P-356).
None is shown by either paper to be sufficient.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: Two community samples of older adults report different MCI prevalences: 21.5% (194 of 902; Singapore, ages 60-99, Petersen criteria with a consensus panel) and 29.3% (314 of 1,071; Fuzhou, ages 55-75, non-depressed, MoCA-based). The gap is well beyond sampling uncertainty (z = 4.0). Differences in diagnostic procedure, sampling frame and country could explain it, but neither paper shows that they do. The ledger's pairing of the prevalence with an odds ratio of 2.581 is a misread.
candidate_explanations: Diagnostic operationalisation: MoCA cut-offs (P-261) against Petersen criteria, 1.5 SD below norms on any test and a consensus panel (P-259). P-259 says its broad battery raises its own estimate, which runs against the gap.
Sampling frame: random draws from the health records of 34 day-care centres in Fuzhou (P-261) against door-to-door and word-of-mouth recruitment in western Singapore (P-259).
Response and missing-data exclusions in P-261: 1071 (58.81%) of the 1821 recruited were analysed.
Sample restrictions in P-261: ages 55-75, self-care ability, GDS-15 > 8 or a history of depression excluded. P-259 took ages 60-99 and included non-ambulant participants. Age runs against the gap.
Country and population: Singapore against Fuzhou, China. P-259 cites a range of 5-36.7% under a uniform criterion.
Neither paper shows any of these to be sufficient.

grounds: Different endpoints: P-41's positive class combines conversion between months 18 and 48 with 15 patients already diagnosed with AD (96 per class), against participants stable to month 48; P-65 predicts conversion within 36 months against participants stable for 36 months.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For predicting progression from normal cognition to MCI in ADNI from baseline hippocampal MRI, P-132 reports a test accuracy of 0.74 (26 of 35; 7-year horizon; 25 stable to 10 progressors). P-177 reports 0.92 (leave-one-out over 60 amnestic-MCI progressors and 60 matched non-progressors; about a 2-year horizon). The gap is beyond combined uncertainty (z = 2.27). Horizon, the extreme-group matched design, class balance, features and validation are candidate explanations, and neither paper shows any of them to be sufficient.
candidate_explanations: Horizon: 7 years (P-132) against about 2 years (P-177).
Extreme-group design: amnestic-MCI progressors against matched non-progressors unimpaired for at least 4 years (P-177), against all NC with 7-year follow-up (P-132).
Scan timing conditioned on outcome: P-177 took progressor scans 2 years before decline.
Class balance: 25:10, with printed F1 implying almost no progressors detected (P-132), against 60:60 (P-177).
Features: radiomics plus ADAS-Cog (P-132) against surface morphometry with sparse coding (P-177). P-177's volume baseline scores 0.72 in its own design.
Validation and size: a 35-subject held-out split (P-132) against LOOCV on 120 (P-177), with small samples named as a limitation.

So the plain version of the method is within uncertainty of P-185. That is the C-147/C-155/C-117 convention, which the advocate itself accepted, and under it condition 3 fails. The reader's verdict stands. If the operator does not count a within-paper ablation under condition 3, the headline figures pass (z = 3.80).

conflicts.claim_a: P-516: Acc ~50% at convergence (ACC decreases as order n increases; exact values figure-only) on T1
conflicts.claim_b: P-523: Acc 87.40% (MCPC; sens 90.48%, spec 84.38%) on T1
conflicts.resolution: Rejected at G4: non-contradiction (MCPC is first-order)
conflicts.resolution_note: Bridging evidence: P-516 reports Acc ~50% at convergence (ACC decreases as order n increases; exact values figure-only) with comparable task/dataset family. Bridging evidence: P-523 reports Acc 87.40% (MCPC; sens 90.48%, spec 84.38%) with comparable task/dataset family. | G4 REVIEWED 2026-07-31 -> NON-CONTRADICTION (false positive). The operator confirmed C-226 conditionally, gated on whether P-523's MCPC constructs higher-order network features. VERIFIED AGAINST summaries.md: MCPC = 'Multiple Connection Pattern Combination', which fuses three FIRST-ORDER connectivity estimators computed directly from BOLD time series over 116 AAL ROIs -- Pearson's correlation (functional), sparse representation (partial correlation), and Granger causality mapping (effective) -- via a multi-kernel SVM. There is no correlation-of-correlations and no PCn recursion, so MCPC is first-order and the operator's own rule reclassifies this as a non-contradiction. The papers in fact AGREE: P-516's first-order PC1 baseline is the reference its higher-order networks degrade away from, and P-523's PC alone scores 77.95%. ROOT CAUSE OF THE FALSE POSITIVE: P-516's registry Best_Metric records 'Acc ~50% at convergence', which is not that paper's best result but the ASYMPTOTE OF A DELIBERATE DEGRADATION ABLATION (accuracy falls as order n rises, reaching chance at convergence). P-516's summary states its numeric ACC/AUC values appear only in figures, so no headline accuracy is extractable. Comparing an ablation's worst point against another paper's headline accuracy is a category error in the Best_Metric field, not a disagreement between the papers. Any paper whose Best_Metric holds a negative or ablation result will keep generating this class of spurious conflict. Bridging evidence: P-822 reports AUC 0.71 with comparable task/dataset family.

conflicts.claim_a: P-655: intensified/doubled mobile-application cognitive training (CCT2x, defined as two mobile-application interventions or active application use) is the top-ranked treatment for every cognitive outcome - global cognition SMD 1.21 (95% CI 0.69-1.73) versus CCT 0.80 (0.34-1.27), episodic memory 0.87 versus 0.36, working memory 0.93 versus 0.62 - and ranks first by SUCRA on all three, on T6 evidence synthesis in MCI/dementia
conflicts.claim_b: P-653: within MCI, adding a three-week computerised cognitive training burst before functional skills training produced NO advantage over skills training alone - composite cognition t = 0.86, p = 0.39; VRFCAT completion time t = 0.19, p = 0.85 - and the synergistic combined-training benefit the same group had previously reported (Harvey et al., 2022) was explicitly not reproduced, on T5 randomised trial evidence in MCI (N = 164)
conflicts.resolution: Genuine claim-level conflict: pooled indirect evidence versus a direct randomised head-to-head on the same question, with the trial that anchors the pooled claim superseded by its own follow-up
conflicts.resolution_note: This is a genuine conflict and the strongest one in the P-620..P-667 batch. Same question (does intensifying or combining computerised cognitive training beat single-modality training in MCI?), same population (MCI), same outcome domain (composite/global cognition), same era (searches closing June 2024 and trial published February 2024) - and opposite answers. The decisive detail is the shared provenance: P-655's CCT2x node draws on Harvey 2022 (N = 117, of which only the 55 cognitively-impaired arms entered the pool), and P-653 IS the successor trial from that same group, which randomised MCI participants precisely to combined-versus-single training and found no difference. The conflict therefore cannot be dismissed as population or paradigm mismatch. INTERPRETATION: P-653 supplies its own mechanism for the discrepancy - the time-by-training-sessions interaction was significant for cognition (F = 4.03, p = 0.02) and within MCI more sessions correlated with more improvement (r = 0.28, p < 0.01 for composite cognition; r = 0.24 for VRFCAT), so the apparent CCT2x superiority in the pooled network is consistent with a training-DOSE confound rather than a synergy between training types: arms labelled intensive simply received more exposure. P-653 also notes its revised graduation criterion cut training exposure relative to the earlier trial, which is why the same group's effect shrank. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE for the manuscript: the CCT2x-first hierarchy should not be reported as evidence of a dose-response or synergy without stating that the one direct randomised test of that hypothesis in MCI was null.
conflicts.evaluator_note: Actor/critic pass 2026-07-31. Checked against the FP taxonomy and survives: task_equivalence holds (both target cognitive-training efficacy in MCI); population is MCI in both; the metric types differ (SMD versus t-test on composite z-scores) so no numeric gap_magnitude is computed and this is filed as a claim-level conflict per the METRIC_TYPE_MISMATCH blocking rule; DESIGN_MISMATCH is present (evidence synthesis versus primary RCT) but is the SUBSTANCE of the conflict rather than a confound, since the question at issue is exactly whether indirect pooled evidence survives a direct randomised test.
conflicts.human_evaluation_note: CONFIRMED GENUINE. A genuine, high-value contradiction: pooled indirect evidence versus a direct randomised head-to-head, with shared provenance (P-655's CCT2x node draws on Harvey 2022; P-653 is that group's successor trial), so it cannot be dismissed as population mismatch. The training-dose-confound resolution is elegant and carries a direct manuscript consequence.

conflicts.claim_a: P-655: computerised cognitive training significantly improves activities of daily living, SMD -0.80 (95% CI -1.40 to -0.21), and ranks first for ADLs by SUCRA, on T6 network meta-analysis of 10 mobile-application RCTs in MCI/dementia
conflicts.claim_b: P-642: neither immersive VR nor non-immersive serious games changed activities of daily living - VR MD -0.07 (95% CI -2.23 to 2.07), SG MD -1.34 (95% CI -4.99 to 3.06), both non-significant - on T6 network meta-analysis of 28 VR/serious-game RCTs in MCI
conflicts.resolution: Resolved: sign convention is lower-is-better (source-verified); P-642's ADL null is underpowered, not contradictory
conflicts.resolution_note: Two network meta-analyses of digital cognitive training in MCI, searching to within six months of each other (P-642 to December 2024, P-655 to end of June 2024), reach opposite conclusions on whether the intervention transfers to activities of daily living. On the face of it this is a genuine claim-level conflict on a matched task, population and outcome. It is filed as PARTIAL rather than genuine for one reason: P-655's ADL result cannot be read. That paper states that a lower score represents better activities of daily living, reports CCT at SMD -0.80 (-1.40 to -0.21) and CCT plus progressive resistance training at +0.80 (0.23-1.38), and then describes CCT_PRT in its discussion as especially beneficial for ADLs - so the two active arms carry opposite signs under a stated convention that would make one of them harmful, and the narrative follows the sign that the convention contradicts. Until that is resolved the direction of P-655's ADL effect is indeterminate and the conflict cannot be adjudicated. NOTE the third data point, which does not resolve it either: P-653 reports a genuine improvement in performance-based functional capacity (VRFCAT completion time, d = 0.64) and bills it as the first demonstration of far transfer to untrained functional capacity in MCI - but VRFCAT is a performance-based simulation, not a rating-scale ADL measure, so it is not commensurable with either network's ADL node. ACTION: flag P-655 for source-level re-extraction of its ADL sign convention before this record is closed either way. | C-228 RESOLVED 2026-07-31 by source-level re-extraction of the P-655 PDF (1-s2.0-S0165178125000757-main.pdf; DOI 10.1016/j.psychres.2025.116426 and title both confirmed in-text). THE SIGN CONVENTION IS NOT AMBIGUOUS - it is lower-is-better, and the Fig. 3 caption states it verbatim: 'A lower score represents better activities of daily living and depression.' Three independent internal checks corroborate it. (1) ARITHMETIC: the results text prints the CCT ADL interval as '1.40 to 0.21', which is not a valid interval because the lower bound exceeds the upper - the minus signs were dropped by the PDF text layer, and the true value is -0.80 (-1.40 to -0.21), exactly as the summary recorded it. The same stripping affects the depression row ('0.77 (95 % CI, 1.08 to 0.45)' = -0.77 (-1.08 to -0.45)). CCT_PRT's interval is printed as 0.23-1.38, both bounds positive and internally valid, so its +0.80 is genuine and not a stripping artefact. (2) DEPRESSION DIRECTION: every depression estimate is negative and the paper states 'CCT2x therapies significantly decreased depressive symptoms', so negative = improvement under the same caption. (3) SUCRA: 'In ADLs, CCT ranked the first' - consistent only if the most negative SMD is the best. Under the opposite reading CCT_PRT (+0.80) would have to rank first, and it does not. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE CONFLICT: with the sign resolved, P-655 reports that CCT significantly IMPROVES ADL (SMD -0.80) while CCT_PRT significantly WORSENS it (SMD +0.80). Set against P-642, whose ADL estimates are VR MD -0.07 (-2.23 to 2.07) and SG MD -1.34 (-4.99 to 3.06), this is a significant effect versus an UNDERPOWERED NULL: P-642's serious-games interval spans zero by a factor of four and its point estimate points the SAME way as P-655's CCT result, so P-642 fails to detect an effect rather than contradicting one. Reclassified genuine=No, resolution_status=false_positive, reason UNDERPOWERED_NULL_VS_SIGNIFICANT_EFFECT. SEPARATE FINDING THAT SURVIVES, AND MATTERS MORE THAN THE CONFLICT: P-655's discussion contradicts its own results table. It states 'CCT_PRT was especially beneficial in improving ADLs' while its own Fig. 3a gives CCT_PRT an ADL SMD of +0.80 (0.23-1.38), which under the paper's stated caption is a significant WORSENING of activities of daily living. The narrative reports a possible harm signal as a benefit. Anything in the manuscript that cites P-655 on CCT_PRT and ADLs must use the results table, not the discussion sentence. Logged for the functional-transfer narrative and cross-referenced from ACTOR-G-022.
conflicts.evaluator_note: Actor/critic pass 2026-07-31. Retained deliberately rather than discarded, because the record documents a reporting defect in a 2025 network meta-analysis that would otherwise be pooled into the manuscript's functional-transfer narrative at face value. Also note both networks are star-shaped without closed loops (see ACTOR-G-023), so neither ADL estimate rests on a direct comparison in any case.
conflicts.human_evaluation_note: CONFIRMED AS UNADJUDICABLE. P-655's ADL sign convention is genuinely unreadable as printed (stated lower-is-better, CCT at -0.80 and CCT+PRT at +0.80, narrative describing CCT+PRT as especially beneficial). Source-level re-extraction is the correct next step before this record closes either way.

conflicts.claim_a: P-642: immersive virtual reality produced a significant DECLINE in global cognition versus control - MMSE MD -1.18 (95% CI -2.18 to -0.20) - while non-immersive serious games improved it (MMSE MD 1.63, MoCA MD 2.84), on T6 network meta-analysis in MCI
conflicts.claim_b: P-655: all computerised cognitive-training nodes improved global cognition versus control - CCT2x SMD 1.21 (0.69-1.73), CCT 0.80 (0.34-1.27) - with no node showing decline, on T6 network meta-analysis in MCI/dementia
conflicts.resolution: Rejected: MODALITY_SUBTYPE_MISMATCH - P-655's network contains no immersive-VR node
conflicts.resolution_note: REJECTED as a false positive, retained as a learning record. The apparent contradiction is that one network reports a significant cognitive DECLINE under a digital intervention while the other reports uniform improvement, both in MCI, both on global cognition, both to a 2024 search date. It fails at the modality sub-level, which is precisely the blocking rule in the reason taxonomy. P-655's eight comparison nodes are CCT, CCT2x, CCE, PRT, MED, CCT+MED, CCT+PRT and control, all of them mobile-application or non-immersive computerised training - there is no head-mounted-display immersive-VR arm anywhere in its network. P-642's decline is attributable specifically to immersive head-mounted VR, and P-642's own non-immersive serious-game node (MMSE MD 1.63, MoCA MD 2.84) agrees in direction and rough magnitude with P-655's CCT nodes. So the two papers agree wherever they overlap and differ only where one of them has no data. LESSON, which is why this record is kept: 'digital cognitive training' is not a single modality family for conflict-detection purposes. Immersive VR and non-immersive computerised training behave in OPPOSITE directions on global cognition within a single well-conducted network (P-642), so any gate that codes them into one bucket will keep generating this class of spurious conflict, and any synthesis that pools them will average a real harm signal against a real benefit signal. Recommend adding immersive_VR and non_immersive_CCT as distinct values of modality_subtype in reason_taxonomy.json.
conflicts.evaluator_note: Actor/critic pass 2026-07-31. Reason code MODALITY_SUBTYPE_MISMATCH applies verbatim: same broad modality family code, different specific modality, with the sub-level match failing. The substantive VR-decline finding is not discarded - it is recorded separately as IA-50.
conflicts.human_evaluation_note: CONFIRMED FALSE POSITIVE. The lesson is more valuable than the contradiction: 'digital cognitive training' is not one modality family. The recommendation to split immersive_VR from non_immersive_CCT in reason_taxonomy.json is actionable and urgent.

conflicts.claim_a: P-632: familiarity-based recognition is SPARED in amnestic MCI - intact on the process-dissociation procedure and intact for lifetime familiarity of object concepts - and impaired only for frequency judgments about recently exposed words (Baycrest/Rotman, 24 aMCI vs 24 healthy older adults)
conflicts.claim_b: P-667: familiarity-based recognition is IMPAIRED in MCI - ROC-derived familiarity medians 0.64 (young) / 0.37 (older) / -0.25 (MCI), overall p = 0.002, with reduced discriminate sensitivity (da 0.57, p = 0.001) and a more liberal response bias (B'' 0.07, p = 0.010) (Taiwan, 26 MCI vs 40 older adults vs 40 young adults)
conflicts.resolution: Rejected: the two results are reconcilable on exposure recency, and P-632 supplies the reconciling variable
conflicts.resolution_note: REJECTED as a false positive, retained because the reconciliation is substantive and neither paper cites the other. The headline claims are flatly opposed - familiarity spared versus familiarity impaired in amnestic MCI, both cross-sectional, both against healthy older adults, both purely behavioural with no classifier. But P-632's own result is a DISSOCIATION, not a blanket sparing: familiarity was intact on the process-dissociation procedure and intact for LIFETIME familiarity of object concepts, and impaired specifically for frequency judgments about RECENTLY exposed words. P-667's boundary-extension paradigm probes recognition of scenes presented minutes earlier in the same session - that is, recent laboratory exposure, which is exactly the condition in which P-632 also found familiarity impaired. Aligned on exposure recency the two papers AGREE, and P-632 supplies the moderator (recent versus lifetime exposure) that P-667 does not measure and cannot explain from its own data. This also predicts P-667's otherwise unexplained internal anomaly, which its authors flag and cannot account for: the drawing-phase object-proportion measure failed to separate healthy older adults from MCI while the recognition-phase familiarity estimate separated MCI from young adults - the drawing phase indexes scene-construction gist rather than recent-exposure familiarity. RECOMMENDATION: promote to a complementary finding rather than leaving it as a rejected conflict, since the pairing yields a testable prediction (an MCI familiarity deficit that scales with recency of exposure and vanishes for lifetime familiarity) that neither paper states.
conflicts.evaluator_note: Actor/critic pass 2026-07-31. Not a genuine conflict under the standard that two claims must be unable to both be true: they can both be true, and are, once the recency moderator is applied. Candidate for promotion into complementary.json.
conflicts.human_evaluation_note: CONFIRMED FALSE POSITIVE, AND PROMOTED. Exemplary handling: the apparent conflict dissolves into an exposure-recency moderator that aligns both papers and predicts P-667's own unexplained internal anomaly. Promoted to complementary.json as a model entry; the testable prediction is a genuine scientific contribution.

conflicts.claim_a: P-645: within amyloid-positive late-life-depression MCI, one-year cognitive decline was carried by the SUBTHRESHOLD-depression subgroup (word-list recall p = 0.020, recognition p = 0.012, MMSE p = 0.049) and not by the major-depression subgroup, while the amyloid-negative major-depression subgroup improved (N = 59, Korea University Guro)
conflicts.claim_b: P-646: high-risk depressive symptom burden, dichotomised at a CES-D cut-off, predicts incident MCI at fully adjusted SHR 1.20 (95% CI 1.08-1.34) - a monotone more-symptoms-more-risk framing (N = 9317, US Health and Retirement Study, Waves 4-14)
conflicts.resolution: Rejected: TASK_SUBSTAGE_MISMATCH plus POPULATION_SPECIFICITY - incidence in a general population versus trajectory within an already-depressed clinic cohort
conflicts.resolution_note: REJECTED as a false positive, retained because it is the seed for an open gap. The surface contradiction is a severity-gradient inversion: P-646 treats more depression as more MCI risk, while P-645 finds the MILDER depression stratum declining faster. It fails on two blocking rules simultaneously. TASK_SUBSTAGE_MISMATCH: P-646 estimates NC-to-MCI incidence in a cognitively unimpaired general-population sample, whereas P-645 measures one-year neuropsychological trajectory within patients who already have both MCI and clinically significant depression - different substages of the same disease course, so the two estimands are not comparable. POPULATION_SPECIFICITY: HRS community respondents versus a tertiary memory-clinic late-life-depression cohort that is 86.4% female with subgroups as small as n = 8. The exposures are also not the same variable - a binary CES-D flag versus a DSM-anchored major-versus-subthreshold clinical stratification. WHY IT IS KEPT: the inversion is real even though the conflict is not, and it is the observation that motivates open gap ACTOR-G-018. The two papers cannot be pitted against each other, but together they show that nobody has tested whether the depression-MCI relation is monotone in severity, because the study that dichotomises cannot see the shape and the study that stratifies is not powered to test it.
conflicts.evaluator_note: Actor/critic pass 2026-07-31. Two independent blocking rules fire, so this would have been routed to partial-not-genuine even before the substantive review. Cross-referenced from ACTOR-G-018.
conflicts.human_evaluation_note: CONFIRMED FALSE POSITIVE. Properly blocked on TASK_SUBSTAGE_MISMATCH plus POPULATION_SPECIFICITY. The inversion is real but the conflict is not, and it is correctly retained as the seed for ACTOR-G-018.

conflicts.claim_a: P-344 (ADNI, n=902 MCI, 5 survival learners): 'RSF was the best model, with C-index 0.878 and IBS 0.115' - random survival forests outperformed classical and other ML survival approaches.
conflicts.claim_b: P-309 (NACC UDS 3.0, n=3,674 MCI): validation C-index 0.781 (RSF), 0.781 (XGBoost), 0.798 (Cox) - 'The prediction effects of the XGBoost and RSF models were not better than those of the Cox model.'
conflicts.description: CONFLICT (rescoped): The within-study ranking of machine-learning survival learners against classical Cox regression for MCI-to-AD time-to-event prediction does not replicate across the two corpus studies that run the comparison themselves. SIDE A - P-344 (ADNI, n=902 MCI, 61 baseline variables, five learners: CoxPH/Weibull/CoxEN/GBSA/RSF): `### What are the outcomes? (Results)` "RSF was the best model, with C-index 0.878 and IBS 0.115"; `### Key findings reported` "Random survival forests outperformed classical and other machine-learning survival approaches in this cohort." SIDE B - P-309 (NACC UDS 3.0, n=3,674 MCI, 13 accessible demographic/lifestyle/comorbidity/neuropsychological predictors): `### What are the outcomes? (Results)` "Validation C-index: 0.781 (RSF), 0.781 (XGBoost), 0.798 (Cox)"; and per the verbatim source abstract carried in P-147 `### Key findings reported`, "The prediction effects of the XGBoost and RSF models were not better than those of the Cox model." Both sides: T2, task_substage=MCI_to_AD, Validation_Type=V2 (internal only), population_specificity=general, Modality=Clinical/tabular, Harrell's C-index. NATURE OF THE CONFLICT: a reversal of ORDINAL RANKING ONLY, not of a quantified effect. P-344 does not report its CoxPH C-index, so the size of its RSF-over-Cox margin is unknown; P-309's margin is 0.017 on a single validation split with no confidence interval, and its measured claim is ML NON-SUPERIORITY rather than Cox superiority. OPEN RESOLUTION MECHANISMS, stated on the record's face: (i) different cohorts - ADNI's biomarker-enriched research cohort vs NACC's multi-centre memory-clinic UDS; note this is the FIRST cross-dataset conflict in this KB, as C-80 (P-82/P-3) and C-204 (P-41/P-65) are both within-ADNI; (ii) different predictor breadth - 61 ADNI baseline variables vs 13 accessible clinical/neuropsychological predictors, with modality_subtype='not reported' on both registry rows so the fine modality gate is UNVERIFIED rather than passed; (iii) both rankings are single-split point estimates without uncertainty on the between-model difference. DROPPED FROM THE RECORD: P-13, which fails the modality gate (registry Modality='MRI/PET', modality_subtype='structural_MRI_only') and whose asserted "Cox best in the high-risk stratum" is not stated in any of its fields - only Cox's own C-index 0.844 (95% CI 0.815-0.873) is reported, with no head-to-head against RSF. LINKED DATA-INTEGRITY ACTIONS (independently verified, action them regardless of the conflict verdict): (1) P-147 and P-309 are the SAME publication - Guan T, Shang L, Yang P et al., J Prev Alz Dis 2025;12:100083, DOI 10.1016/j.tjpad.2025.100083, NACC n=3,674, identical C-indices 0.781/0.781/0.798 and IBS 0.087, identical 13 predictors; both registry rows carry duplicate_of='not reported' and one must be set. (2) IA-16 [confirmed, strength "strong"] rests on that single study counted once, and P-344 is unclaimed counter-evidence to it; attach a G5 caveat to IA-16 noting the ordering does not replicate in ADNI. (3) Registry primary_metric_type is mis-coded 'AUC_ROC' for P-147/P-309 and should be 'C_index' - the source reports concordance indices; this mis-coding is the likely reason no automated pass ever paired these papers.
conflicts.source: claude receiver-side mining sweep (Fable 5): 5 band miners over 156 under-mined papers under the FP-hardened rulebook, each candidate then adversarially verified by an independent agent
conflicts.review_note: MINED + INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED (ACCEPT_WITH_RESCOPE, medium). Passes the conflict bar on all four gates: same task substage (MCI_to_AD), comparable validation tier (V2 both), same modality subtype (clinical/tabular), commensurable metric (Harrell C-index). IMPORTANT SCOPE recorded by the verifier: this is a reversal of ORDINAL RANKING ONLY, not of a quantified effect - P-344 does not report its CoxPH C-index so its RSF-over-Cox margin is unknown, and P-309's margin is 0.017 on a single split with no CI. genuine=None pending human G4; do NOT promote to genuine without operator review.

verification.method: mined from under-mined corpus papers under the FP-hardened rulebook, then INDEPENDENTLY adversarially verified (quote-by-quote verbatim audit + field-placement audit + FP-code sweep + dedup)
verification.quote_audit: ALL nine miner quotes checked line-by-line against summaries.md. Every load-bearing quote is VERBATIM and sits in a MEASURED field. (1) P-344 L25669 `### What are the key components in the method?` "ADNI cohort of 902 MCI participants... five survival models: CoxPH, Weibull, CoxEN, GBSA, and RSF." VERBATIM. (2) P-344 L25675 `### What are the outcomes? (Results)` "RSF was the best model, with C-index 0.878 and IBS 0.115, and SHAP showed cognitive tests as the strongest predictors." VERBATIM - MEASURED. (3) P-344 L25702 `### Key findings reported` "Random survival forests outperformed classical and other machine-learning survival approaches in this cohort." VERBATIM - MEASURED. (4) P-309 L22793-94 `### What are the outcomes? (Results)` "Validation C-index: 0.781 (RSF), 0.781 (XGBoost), 0.798 (Cox)." / "IBS reported as 0.087 for Cox; Cox performed best overall." VERBATIM modulo bullet markers - MEASURED. (5) P-309 L22823 `### Key findings reported` "Cox model achieved the best overall performance among tested models." VERBATIM - MEASURED. (6) P-147 L5360 `### Key findings reported` "In the validation set, the concordance indices were 0.781 (RSF), 0.781 (XGBoost), and 0.798 (Cox), and the Integrated Brier Score was 0.087 (Cox). The prediction effects of the XGBoost and RSF models were not better than those of the Cox model." VERBATIM (source has ligature glyphs 'eﬀects') - MEASURED. (7) P-309 L22784-87 method components - VERBATIM. (8+9) P-13 L13423-24 `### What are the outcomes? (Results)` "For the high-risk group, Cox model performance reached **C-index 0.844 (95% CI: 0.815-0.873)**." and "RSF with longitudinal ADAS13/FAQ plus demographics and APOE e4 was favored for low-risk prognosis." VERBATIM - MEASURED field. CREDIT: the miner deliberately avoided P-309's interpretiv
verification.fp_findings: PASSES: SOURCE_REFUSES_CONCLUSION - I read both `### Potential gaps or limitations` fields; P-344 "Feature set and cohort are ADNI-specific, with limited external validation", P-309 "Limited extract detail on metrics and validation beyond internal testing". Both limit external generalisability; NEITHER retracts its own within-study model ranking. PASSES: SCOPE_POOLED_POPULATION - both cohorts are pure MCI (902 MCI; 3,674 MCI subjects), no dementia pooling. PASSES: MODEL_FITTED_VALUE_AS_MEASURED - C-indices are validation-set discrimination, not fitted values at chosen covariate levels. PASSES: AUTHORS_DECLINED_TO_CLAIM - both rankings are headlined in the papers' own Key findings / abstract Conclusion, not buried in Open problems. PASSES: FAILS_SOURCE_OWN_CORRECTION - N/A, no multiple-comparison p-values involved. PASSES: DEDUP - I loaded all 165 records in data/conflicts.json and matched on paper_a/paper_b: the ONLY record touching any of these is C-187 (P-344 vs P-192, C-index 0.878 vs PPV 68.0, genuine_conflict=false, incommensurable metrics). No record pairs P-344 with P-309 or P-147. Not one of the 3 genuine conflicts. Distinct from IA-16 (verified in invalidated.json: IA-16 paper_id='P-147', status confirmed, single-paper evidence base) - this is the counter-evidence to that IA, not a restatement. TRIPS (all fixable by rescope): (a) EVIDENTIAL_OVERSTATEMENT on P-13 - "Cox best in the high-risk stratum" is inferred, not in any field. (b) UNQUANTIFIED_REVERSAL_CLAUSE, partial - side A's RSF-vs-Cox margin carries NO statistic because P-344's Cox C-index is never reported; only the ordinal "best of five" is measured. (c) Side B is mis-framed: the source's measured claim is NON-SUPERIORITY ("not better than"), margin 0.017 on a single split with no CI - "Cox was best"
verification.verifier_reason: ACCEPT WITH RESCOPE. What survives adversarial scrutiny is the strongest thing a conflict can have in this KB and the reason I did not reject: BOTH sides ran the Cox-vs-ML comparison THEMSELVES, inside their own cohort. conflicts.claim_a: P-832 (Teselink et al. 2021, Ageing Res Rev 72:101499; NIBS meta-analysis, 19 studies for global cognition): the tDCS subgroup did NOT significantly improve global cognition - SMD 1.20 (95% CI -0.26, 2.65), I2 93.6%, p = 0.107, from 6 studies (94 active / 78 sham). The abstract states the effects were 'restricted to rTMS but not tDCS'.
conflicts.claim_b: P-705 (tDCS meta-analysis for global cognition in MCI and AD, 22 RCTs / 1,074 patients, 426 MCI and 648 AD): tDCS DID improve global cognition - MMSE pooled mean difference 1.96 points (95% CI 0.95 to 2.97), p = 0.0001, from 10 RCTs in 9 studies with 451 participants, random-effects, I2 92%.
conflicts.description: CONFLICT (curated at G4 2026-08-23; Agent 4 did not detect it). Two meta-analyses of transcranial direct-current stimulation for GLOBAL COGNITION in overlapping MCI/AD populations reach opposite conclusions about whether tDCS works. P-832 finds the tDCS subgroup non-significant (SMD 1.20, 95% CI -0.26 to 2.65, p = 0.107) and concludes efficacy is restricted to rTMS; P-705 finds tDCS significantly improves MMSE (MD 1.96, 95% CI 0.95 to 2.97, p = 0.0001). NOT a metric-incommensurability artefact of the kind rejected elsewhere in this ledger: the disagreement is about the SIGNIFICANCE and direction of a synthesis, not about comparing an SMD to an MD numerically. The two reviews also draw on overlapping primary trials, which makes this the informative 'same evidence, different synthesis' case - plausible sources are P-832's smaller tDCS subgroup (6 studies) versus P-705's 10 RCTs, differing inclusion windows, and P-832 pooling any global-cognition instrument while P-705 pools MMSE specifically. Both carry extreme heterogeneity (I2 93.6% and 92%), which is itself the most defensible reading: neither pooled estimate is stable. SIGN NOTE: P-832's lower bound is printed as ' 0.26' with the minus lost in extraction; it is reconstructed as -0.26 on two independent anchors - the point estimate is the interval midpoint only if the bound is negative (1.195 vs 1.455), and the printed p = 0.107 requires an interval crossing zero.
conflicts.modality_family: non-invasive brain stimulation (tDCS) intervention, global cognition outcome
conflicts.apparent_performance_gap: significant vs non-significant pooled effect for the same intervention and outcome
conflicts.resolution: unresolved - both pooled estimates carry I2 > 92%
conflicts.resolution_note: Curated by the delegated evaluator at G4 for batch P-828..P-837. Recommend surfacing in the review paper as a synthesis-level disagreement with the heterogeneity caveat, NOT as evidence that one review is wrong. See also PAPERINGO-ha4: reviews in this corpus routinely re-pool the same trials, so agreement between two meta-analyses is not independent confirmation and disagreement is not necessarily a data conflict.

conflicts.claim_a: P-989 (Yoon et al. 2023, Front Aging Neurosci 14:1051621; Seoul aMCI cohort n=1,184, 3.1y): two-step clustering of NPI-Q-derived MBI domains yields a complex multi-domain group (23.2%) whose AD progression hazard is 2.541x the asymptomatic group [1.904-3.392] - prognostic signal lives in the co-occurrence STRUCTURE of the symptom profile (aggregation architecture).
conflicts.claim_b: P-997 (Meng et al. 2023, CNS Neurosci Ther 29:2259-2266; PPMI early PD n=423, 5y): domain-resolved mixed-effects modelling shows ICDs accelerate memory decline yet do NOT raise MCI occurrence, while depression/anxiety span all four domains - prognostic signal lives in the symptom-to-outcome MAPPING, not in symptom count (decomposition architecture).
conflicts.description: CONFLICT (Actor-detected, Critic-survived, G4 delegated 2026-08-28). Two longitudinal cohorts address the same architectural question - how should neuropsychiatric symptoms be organised for cognitive prognosis - with structurally opposed answers. P-989's aggregation architecture treats the symptom VECTOR as the unit (more co-occurring domains = higher hazard, dose-response); P-997's decomposition architecture treats symptom-outcome PAIRS as the unit (ICD-memory coupling exists even though ICDs do not raise MCI occurrence, so a count-based aggregation would average the specificity away). This is not a population artefact to be dismissed: both cohorts model NPS against cognitive deterioration with comparable longitudinal designs; the clash is in the representational geometry of the feature space. A count-aggregating model fit to P-997's data would dilute the ICD-memory signal into the profile mean, and a domain-decomposing model fit to P-989's data would miss the co-occurrence interaction that carries the 2.5x hazard. The conflict predicts a falsifiable test: neither architecture should transfer unchanged across the two cohorts.
conflicts.task_equivalence: both model NPS against cognitive deterioration in longitudinal cohorts (risk stratification vs decline-rate decomposition)
conflicts.dataset_family_equivalence: single-centre Korean aMCI cohort vs multinational PPMI early-PD cohort - distinct datasets, shared construct (NPS)
conflicts.modality_family: both clinical/neuropsychiatric questionnaire cohorts (NPI-Q-derived MBI vs NPS batteries)
conflicts.apparent_performance_gap: not a metric gap: 2.541x hazard (aggregation) vs domain-specific mixed-effects betas (decomposition) are incommensurable by construction
conflicts.resolution: Both architectures are internally valid; the conflict marks an open modelling question, not an error in either paper.
conflicts.resolution_note: Architectural interpretation: the corpus holds a representational fork for NPS prognostication - profile-aggregation (unsupervised clustering, P-989) versus domain-decomposition (per-outcome mixed effects, P-997). They make different predictions under feature transfer: aggregation presumes exchangeable symptom contributions within a profile, decomposition presumes outcome-specific pathways. The 2.541x hazard of the complex-MBI group and the ICD-specific memory decline with null MCI occurrence are both real findings; their joint lesson is that NPS prognostic architectures must be selected by the target outcome (conversion hazard vs domain trajectory), not by habit. Head-to-head evaluation on a cohort with both MBI clustering inputs and domain-level cognitive outcomes is the missing experiment (cf. ACTOR-G-082..085 territory).

conflicts.claim_a: P-988 (Parra et al. 2022, Alzheimers Dement DADM 14:e12386; Argentina n=107, 40-month follow-up): a ~10-minute task-embedded eye-tracking test (VSTMB) prospectively predicts MCI-to-ADS conversion with 94% of baseline-predicted progressors converting and 0% of non-predicted - near-perfect prospective separation from a brief behavioural test.
conflicts.claim_b: P-991 (Tokaj & Lehrner 2024, Neuropsychiatr 38:71-81; Vienna n=622, follow-up n=117): none of three brief paper-based tests (MMSE, Sunderland CDT, VVT 3.0) adequately predicts disease progression, and none discriminates all four stages (HC/SCD/MCI/AD) - a direct negative result on brief-screen prognostic sufficiency.
conflicts.description: CONFLICT (Actor-detected, Critic-survived, G4 delegated 2026-08-28). Both studies ask whether a brief (<15 min) clinic assessment can carry prognostic signal across the AD continuum, and reach opposite verdicts. P-991's null (three standard brief tests fail progression prediction in a 622-patient cohort) versus P-988's near-ceiling positive (94%-vs-0% 40-month separation from a brief digital test). The Critic first tested the trivial escape - different outcomes - and rejected it: P-991's progression arm is genuinely prospective prediction (117 follow-ups), the same quantity P-988 targets. The conflict is architectural: static single-timepoint neuropsychological SCALING (scores as trait summaries) versus task-embedded PROCESS-TRACING (oculomotor behaviour during a memory-binding probe as a state readout). The signal P-991 cannot find in scores is exactly what P-988 extracts from behaviour-during-task - the predictive information lives in the dynamics of the measurement episode, not in its summary score. This reframes 'brief tests fail at prognosis' as 'brief STATIC tests fail': measurement episode design, not test brevity, is the operative variable.
conflicts.task_equivalence: both evaluate brief clinic assessments for prospective progression/conversion prediction
conflicts.dataset_family_equivalence: Argentine clinic cohort vs Austrian memory-clinic cohort - distinct sites, same clinical question
conflicts.modality_family: behavioural assessment (digital oculomotor vs paper-based neuropsychology)
conflicts.apparent_performance_gap: 94%-vs-0% prospective separation (P-988) vs 'none adequate' progression prediction (P-991)
conflicts.resolution: Both findings stand; the conflict localises the predictive signal to task-embedded dynamics rather than summary scores.
conflicts.resolution_note: Architectural interpretation: the pair splits the corpus's brief-assessment philosophy. Static scaling (MMSE/CDT/VVT) compresses the measurement episode into a trait score and, per P-991, loses the prognostic dynamics; process-tracing (VSTMB eye tracking) samples the episode itself and, per P-988, retains near-deterministic conversion information. The falsifiable consequence: paper-based static tests matched for duration to the VSTMB should still underperform it on prospective conversion, and VSTMB-style dynamics extracted from paper tasks (drawing kinematics) should partially close the gap. Either outcome resolves the conflict; neither is currently in the corpus.
conflicts.demotion_note_2026_08_29: Demoted to candidate 2026-08-29 (data-quality audit): Task_Type T2 vs T1 and all four deterministic gates fail (eye-tracking VSTMB conversion vs paper MMSE/CDT/VVT discrimination); the record says 'Both findings stand' and its P-991 half is simultaneously the sole basis of confirmed IA-88. Promoted 2026-08-28 by a delegated evaluator with no human gate. A human G4 may re-admit it with an explicit g4_override.

readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_b: Prognostic value of baseline MMSE, Sunderland CDT and VVT 3.0 Screening scores: for progression to the next diagnostic stage (HC, SCD, MCI, AD) over 12-48 months among 117 returners (Mann-Whitney on baseline scores), and for MCI-to-AD in 76 MCI patients (ROC AUC); Vienna memory clinic, retrospective analysis.
grounds: The record's own resolution presents both findings as true ('Both findings stand') and attributes the difference to static test scores versus task-embedded eye movements. That is an 'architectural fork', which the rule records as a false positive (record resolution; P-988 p3 and P-991 p6 quotes show the different instruments).

The two papers evaluate different instruments: P-988 its VSTMB eye-tracking model, P-991 the MMSE, Sunderland CDT and VVT 3.0. Neither tests or makes any claim about the other's instrument, so a positive result for one and a null for the others is a claim about X set against a claim about Y (P-988 p3 quotes; P-991 p6 quotes).

The record misreads P-991 as a blanket null on brief-test prognosis. Within MCI, the MMSE reached AUC 0.808, and the authors conclude that the MMSE 'showed some validity'. On the record's own question, whether a brief clinic test can carry prognostic signal, both papers therefore answer in the same direction (P-991 p6 and p10 quotes; P-988 p7 quote).

The record says P-991's progression arm is 'genuinely prospective prediction' and 'the same quantity P-988 targets'. P-991 contradicts this: it is a retrospective analysis, and its progression endpoint is conversion to the next stage over 12-48 months among 117 returners (P-991 p3 and p6 quotes).

It could not be genuine in any case. As a prognostic-performance comparison, it rests on P-988's near-ceiling in-sample discrimination (AUC 1.0; 63 of 65 classified correctly) in 65 patients at one site with no external cohort (P-988 p1 and p7 quotes).
