conflicts.claim_a: Arm A - plasma galectin-3 nomogram for MCI in T2DM inpatients at Affiliated Zhongda Hospital (Southeast University), n=329, evaluated on a held-out 30 percent split (AUC 0.813 training / 0.775 validation). Supplies the lower discrimination value and the stronger validation procedure.
conflicts.claim_b: Arm B - plasma BVR-A + HOMA-IR + diabetes-duration nomogram for MCI in T2DM inpatients at Affiliated Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University, n=140, evaluated by 5-fold cross-validation inside the derivation sample (C-index 0.863, 95% CI 0.752-0.937). Supplies the higher discrimination value, the weaker validation procedure, and the untested ranking claim that disqualifies it as a strong arm.
conflicts.conflict_statement: DOCUMENTED INCOMMENSURABILITY, NOT A GENUINE CONFLICT (route to partial). The apparent 0.088-point discrimination advantage of the biliverdin-reductase-A + HOMA-IR + diabetes-duration nomogram (P-1212, C-index 0.863) over the galectin-3 + age + education nomogram (P-1206, AUC 0.775 on its held-out split) for detecting MCI in hospitalised type 2 diabetes patients must not be promoted to a genuine conflict, even though the pair passes every hard comparability gate. Three reasons: (1) the two nomograms were derived on different single-centre Chinese inpatient cohorts (Xuzhou Medical University, n=140, 65 NCF / 75 MCI; Affiliated Zhongda Hospital Southeast University, n=329 split 7:3) from disjoint candidate-predictor sets, and neither paper measured or tested the other's marker, so there is no head-to-head and no disagreement in direction - each reports its own marker as independently associated with MCI in T2DM; (2) the two numbers were produced by different validation procedures - 0.863 is resampled (5-fold cross-validation) inside the same 140-patient derivation sample that fitted the three predictors, while 0.775 is measured on 98 patients held out of fitting - so the higher value comes from the procedure with the greater optimism, and the ordering is at least as consistent with in-sample optimism as with marker superiority; (3) P-1212 additionally cannot serve as the strong arm because its own ranking claim ('BVR-A had the highest diagnostic efficiency among the studied indicators') is made with no reported test comparing BVR-A's discrimination against HOMA-IR or diabetes duration. Separately, the METRIC_TYPE_MISMATCH warning gatecheck raises on this pair (AUC_ROC vs C_index) is a registry coding artefact rather than a real incommensurability: for a binary-outcome logistic nomogram Harrell's C-index and the ROC-AUC are the same statistic. The pair is therefore blocked for the wrong reason by the deterministic gate and would be promoted for the wrong reason by a gap-magnitude rule.

conflicts.claim_a: The observed arm. Reports the directly measured 36-month societal-cost trajectory of the GERAS-US MCI and mild-AD strata, which is highest at baseline and then declines; establishes that no aggregate cost escalation accompanied the cohort's documented MMSE and CFI decline.
conflicts.claim_b: The modelled arm. Reports the fitted MMSE-change-to-cost/caregiver-time/HRQoL association in the same cohort and the 20-30 percent progression-slowing simulation built on those coefficients; supplies the +$8,504 and $2,638 figures that the corpus would otherwise carry as observed burden and observed saving.
conflicts.conflict_statement: DOCUMENTED INCOMMENSURABILITY, EXPLICITLY NOT A GENUINE CONFLICT. The corpus holds two health-economic records drawn from the SAME GERAS-US 36-month early-AD cohort, with the same first author, that point in opposite directions on whether progression produces observable cost escalation in MCI - and they must not be cited alongside each other as mutually reinforcing evidence for the value of slowing progression. P-1000 reports the directly observed trajectory: total societal costs in the MCI stratum FELL over the 36 months, from about $2,430 to $2,007 per month. P-1093 reports a modelled increment in the same cohort: natural 36-month MCI progression 'associated with' +$8,504 in societal costs, from which it projects $2,638 per-person savings from a 30 percent slowing of progression. The +$8,504 is a coefficient from a fitted GLM relating MMSE change to cost in an outcome subset of 222 of 617 enrolled participants; it is not an observed cost rise, and the same cohort's own aggregate cost trajectory contains no rise for it to correspond to. This pair CANNOT be upgraded to a genuine conflict: the two papers share participants and a first author, so they are one body of evidence rather than two independent arms, and gatecheck FAILs four gates. The record's purpose is citation hygiene - any synthesis that quotes P-1093's $8,504 or $2,638 as measured burden or measured saving is presenting a model-fitted quantity as an observation that its own source cohort did not make.

conflicts.residual_risk: The two quantities are not logically contradictory, and a gate may reasonably judge the record too thin on that basis. A positive WITHIN-PERSON association between MMSE decline and cost (P-1093) is fully compatible with falling COHORT-MEAN monthly costs (P-1000) if the cost profile is baseline-heavy, if attrition is differential (P-1093 itself analyses only 222 of 617), and if pandemic service disruption suppressed resource use in the later follow-up windows - all three are documented for this cohort. If that reconciliation is accepted, what remains is a citation hazard rather than a substantive disagreement: P-1093's $8,504 and $2,638 are correctly labelled as modelled by their own authors, and only a downstream synthesis that strips that label creates the problem. A second, weaker objection: P-1000's cost trend is reported as 'broadly stable' with no test statistic in the digest, so the observed arm's direction is itself untested.

conflicts.claim_a: The apparent positive arm. MCI-only (Petersen / DSM-5, age 60+), single-modality aerobic exercise, 11 RCTs, pooled global-cognition SMD 0.76 with the 95 percent CI printed inconsistently (0.37-1.14 in the abstract, 0.37-0.91 in the Results). Its prediction interval runs -0.63 to 2.15, and its two dosing moderator claims rest on non-significant between-group tests, so its headline cannot serve as the strong arm of anything.
conflicts.claim_b: The apparent null arm, and the reason the pair is incommensurable. Exergaming RCTs pooling MCI AND dementia in one cognitive estimate (166 MCI across 4 trials, 350 dementia across 6 trials), primary MMSE MD 0.95 (95 percent CI -1.17 to 3.08, P = 0.38). Also the only paper of the two that directly tests cognitively loaded exercise, and its own open problem list names the missing MCI-versus-dementia stratification and the missing dose-matched comparator.
conflicts.conflict_statement: DOCUMENTED INCOMMENSURABILITY, NOT A GENUINE CONFLICT - and the reason matters more than the block. Two meta-analyses published in the SAME journal volume (Geriatric Nursing 51, 2023) reach opposite headline verdicts on whether exercise-class intervention improves global cognition in MCI: P-698 reports a significant pooled SMD 0.76 for aerobic exercise, while P-699's PRIMARY pooled MMSE for exergaming across 5 studies is null at MD 0.95 (95 percent CI -1.17 to 3.08, P = 0.38). The pair must not be promoted. (1) It fails the deterministic population gate: P-699's evidence base is 166 MCI participants across 4 trials pooled together with 350 dementia participants across 6 trials, whereas P-698 is restricted to adults 60+ meeting Petersen / DSM-5 MCI criteria - so P-699's null is not an MCI null, and P-699 itself lists 'whether the cognitive benefits survive when MCI and dementia are analysed separately' as an open problem. (2) The metric types are not commensurable: a standardised Hedges' g against raw MMSE points. (3) Neither arm is usable as the strong arm, because each is independently flagged for asserting in its abstract what its own results table does not support (P-699: 'the abstract does not match the results table'; P-698: the dosing claims rest on between-group tests it reports as non-significant). The substantive point the pair looks like it settles - does adding cognitive load to aerobic exercise add value in MCI - is in fact UNTESTED on both sides: P-698's cognitive-factors contrast (1.04 vs 0.37) has a between-group meta-ANOVA of Q(1) = 2.91, p = 0.09, and P-699's cognitively loaded arm (exergaming) is null on its primary MMSE pool and turns positive only after post-hoc removal of Padala 2012. Record as an incommensurable pair plus a named untested question, not as a conflict.

That re-pool is not in the corpus and cannot be done from the digests (P-699 never identifies which two of its ten trials were dropped from the meta-analysis), but this record should be revisited if it ever is. A second, independent risk runs the other way: non_independence_report.md flags that both papers pool exercise-class RCTs in MCI and that trial overlap has never been checked, so even a repaired population match could leave the two non-independent and therefore still unusable as two arms.

P-699's MCI-only global-cognition estimate is a different pool (MoCA MD, 3 MCI trials).
grounds: Both headline estimates favour the intervention (P-698 SMD 0.76, significant; P-699 MMSE MD 0.95, 95% CI -1.17 to 3.08, P = 0.38), so the claimed opposition is a significance-only difference, which Section 5.2 says is not a data conflict.

P-699's own headline is positive: its abstract reports a significant difference on MMSE and MoCA and its conclusion says exergaming improves cognition in older adults with MCI or dementia, so the reviews do not reach opposite verdicts.

P-699's null MMSE pool is four dementia trials plus one MCI trial, while its only MCI-only global-cognition pool (MoCA: Amjad 2019, Liao 2020, Liu 2022) shows a significant benefit (MD 2.12, 0.53-3.70), the same direction as P-698.
The record misreads P-699: the paper names no primary outcome, and the 'open problem' and 'abstract does not match the results table' sentences the record quotes are not in the PDF.

Were there a disagreement, the quantities would still differ: aerobic exercise against non-exercise controls on a standardised scale versus exergaming against mostly traditional physical activity or usual care on MMSE points, in MCI versus a mostly dementia pool, with the dataset-family gate unmatched.

record_defects: conflict_statement: the two reviews do not 'reach opposite headline verdicts'; P-699's abstract reports a significant difference on MMSE and MoCA and its conclusion states that exergaming improves cognition in older adults with MCI or dementia (with a caution for heterogeneity).
conflict_statement and claim_b call the MMSE pool P-699's 'PRIMARY' cognitive estimate; P-699 designates no primary outcome and reports the MMSE and MoCA pools side by side.

The record omits P-699's MCI-only MoCA pool (3 MCI trials, MD 2.12, 95% CI 0.53-3.70, P = 0.009), which agrees in direction with P-698; the null MMSE pool is four dementia trials plus one MCI trial (Amjad 2019).

claim_b ('pooling MCI AND dementia in one cognitive estimate (166 MCI across 4 trials, 350 dementia across 6 trials)'): those counts describe the 10 included trials; no single cognitive pool combines them (MMSE: 5 trials, 1 in MCI; MoCA: 3 trials, all MCI).

conflicts.claim_a: The high arm and the one whose evidence base is selected. 23 controlled exercise studies admitted only if they reported a quantitative cognitive assessment AND neuroinflammatory/neuroprotective blood markers; amnestic MCI excluded from the quantitative synthesis; pooled global effect SMD 1.165 with I-squared 88.045 percent and a prediction interval crossing zero. conflicts.claim_b: The low arm and the methodologically tighter one. 25 RCTs reported across 38 papers, multilevel random-effects modelling with effect sizes nested within study and trial plus a Bayesian network, giving aerobic-without-music g = 0.48 from 11 trials and 683 participants. It is not an independent replication of P-680: it draws its trial pool from its own team's prior overview of reviews of the same literature, and its own headline (AEwM g = 1.2 on 2 trials) is separately overclaim-flagged, so it can
conflicts.conflict_statement: DOCUMENTED INCOMMENSURABILITY, NOT A GENUINE CONFLICT - and the only pair in this pack that PASSES all four deterministic conflict gates, so the gate cannot stop it and a human rule must. P-680 pools the global effect of exercise on cognition in MCI at SMD 1.165 (95 percent CI 0.741 to 1.589), with aerobic exercise specifically at 1.442 (95 percent CI 0.642 to 2.260, df = 5); P-683 independently pools aerobic exercise without music at g = 0.48 (95 percent CI 0.18 to 0.79) from 26 effect sizes across 11 trials and 683 participants - a magnitude discrepancy of roughly three-fold on the same population (MCI), the same outcome domain (global cognition), the same intervention family and an overlapping era. It is NOT a conflict, for three reasons none of which the gate can see. (1) The two syntheses AGREE in direction, and even the aerobic-versus-aerobic intervals still overlap between 0.642 and 0.79, so no incompatible conclusion exists to adjudicate. (2) They are not independent replications: both re-pool an overlapping published trial literature (P-683's evidence base is drawn from its own team's prior overview of reviews plus a supplementary search), and neither digest preserves its trial roster, so shared primary trials cannot be excluded. (3) The discrepancy is attributable to documented SELECTION decisions inside P-680 rather than to any disagreement about the trials: P-680 required every included study to report neuroinflammatory or neuroprotective blood markers alongside cognition, and it excluded 4 amnestic-MCI studies (259 participants) from the quantitative synthesis - so its 23-study base is a biomarker-reporting subset of non-amnestic MCI trials, not the exercise literature. P-680's own prediction interval of -0.747 to 3.077 includes zero, and P-680 is overclaim-flagged, so it cannot be the strong arm of anything. The usable corpus content is a caution, not a conflict: in this corpus the MAGNITUDE of a pooled exercise-cognition effect in MCI tracks the synthesis's inclusion filter and pooling model, and a pair of reviews differing three-fold is evidence about synthesis method, not about exercise.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: Two meta-analyses of aerobic exercise against control in older adults with MCI report effects on cognition that differ beyond combined uncertainty. P-680 reports an SMD of 1.442 (95% CI 0.624-2.260; 5 studies, composite of all cognitive tests), and P-683 reports 0.48 (0.18-0.79; 11 RCTs, global cognition, aerobic exercise without music) (z = 2.16). The margin is thin: P-683's figures nearer P-680's class mix or quality restriction (0.53, 0.57 and 0.6) give z = 1.88-2.00. P-680's broader 'aerobic' class (it includes a music-accompanied trial and a dance trial), its no-exercise comparators, its composite outcome, its exclusion of amnestic trials and its heterogeneity are candidate explanations, none shown to be sufficient.
candidate_explanations: Intervention class: P-680's aerobic stratum includes Song & Yu 2019, which P-683 classes as aerobic with music (g = 1.2), and Qi 2019, which P-683 classes as dance.
Comparator: P-680 required a no-exercise condition. P-683's controls include balance, stretching or toning (N = 7), a home exercise programme and low-intensity non-aerobic exercise.
Outcome construct: P-680 pools a composite of all cognitive domains, P-683 the global-cognition domain. This may run against the gap.
Population: P-680 left amnestic MCI out of its analysis; P-683's AEwtM node includes amnestic trials.
Design: P-683 admits full-length RCTs only; P-680 also admits non-randomised controlled studies.
Evidence base and heterogeneity: P-680 has 5 studies with I2 of 89%; P-683 has 11 trials and 26 effect sizes in a multilevel model.
Change-SD standardisation: P-683 imputes missing change SDs with r = 0.68; P-680 does not state its pre-post correlation.
Neither paper shows any of these to be sufficient.

conflicts.conflict_statement: DOCUMENTED INCOMMENSURABILITY, NOT PROPOSED AS A GENUINE CONFLICT. Three exercise-for-MCI syntheses in this pack each nominate a DIFFERENT optimal exercise modality - aerobic (P-845), resistance (P-848) and combined (P-1131) - and all three pairings print 'PASS - eligible to propose as a genuine-conflict candidate' from gatecheck.py because modality_subtype and task_substage are 'not reported' on these rows and every hard gate matches (T6, review_meta_analysis, general). The disagreement is nevertheless unadjudicable and must not be promoted: the three rankings are over DIFFERENT outcome domains (P-845 memory and independent living, P-848 neuropsychiatric symptoms, P-1131 global cognition); two of the three compute no effect estimate of any kind, so there is no second arm to weigh; all three carry authors_overclaim for asserting a modality ranking with no between-modality statistical test; and two of the three pool MCI participants together with AD or dementia participants, so no MCI-specific ordering is estimable. The operative blocking rule for the pipeline: 'exercise' is not one modality family, and a top-ranked modality is meaningless without naming the outcome domain it was ranked on.

conflicts.residual_risk: The record may be judged redundant. VF-30 already states that cross-intervention rankings in MCI are not trustworthy, and if the operator treats VF-30 as binding on the pair-generator then all this adds is three paper ids and the gate transcript. A second, sharper objection: P-848 is not actually in the same class as the other two - it is a 34-study, 3655-participant network meta-analysis with a real pooled estimate and confidence interval, while P-845 and P-1131 pool nothing at all. A reviewer could therefore rule that there is no conflict here for the ordinary reason that there is only ever ONE arm, and that dressing that up as an 'incommensurability' overstates it. A third: the three reviews plausibly share included primary trials (P-845 charts 34 trials, P-848 34 studies over 2007-2025, P-1131 10 international RCTs), which neither gatecheck nor the non-independence registry records - if the overlap is substantial they are not three independent syntheses either, which would be a fourth blocking reason but also weakens any framing of this as a three-way disagreement.

conflicts.claim_a: The high-AUC arm. Cross-sectional Simoa plasma p-tau181 study, 79 patients (33 SCD, 32 MCI, 14 AD-dementia), 72 with CSF, A/T(N) classification with AP+ = A+ and T+, ROC with Youden cut-off. It supplies both the 0.910 figure and, in its own comparison with prior work, the explanation for why that figure exceeds the published range.
conflicts.claim_b: The pooled arm. PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis of 150 studies (137 quantitative), random-effects ratio-of-means with QUADAS-2, searched to 17 May 2021. It supplies the synthesised P-tau181 accuracy range and, critically, the different target condition (aMCI/AD versus controls) that the range is an accuracy for.
conflicts.conflict_statement: DOCUMENTED INCOMMENSURABILITY, NOT A GENUINE CONFLICT. The corpus holds two plasma p-tau181 discrimination figures that look directly comparable - same analyte, same metric type (AUC), overlapping symptomatic populations, both non-ADNI - and are not. P-1225 reports AUC 0.910 for plasma p-tau181 in a Florence memory-clinic sample of 79 SCD/MCI/AD-dementia patients, but its target condition is biomarker-defined AD-pathology carriage inside an already-symptomatic sample: AP+ is A+ and T+ regardless of N, so the ROC separates pathology-positive from pathology-negative patients, not patients from controls. P-1231's 150-study meta-analysis pools P-tau181 diagnostic accuracy at AUC 0.61-0.84 for a different target condition, clinically defined amnestic MCI or AD versus controls. The single-site value therefore sits above the entire synthesised range without contradicting it, and P-1225's own discussion supplies the reason. The reusable point is structural: the registry has no target-condition column, so nothing in the coded record distinguishes 'discriminates biomarker-positive from biomarker-negative within a symptomatic cohort' from 'discriminates cases from controls', and any future automated pass over blood-biomarker AUCs in this corpus will regenerate this pair as an apparent conflict.

challenge.by: second model reader instructed to argue the verdict into a genuine contradiction (or out of one), reading both source documents in full
challenge.strongest_case_against_the_verdict: Three routes, the second and third on quantities the ledger record did not name. (a) Same analyte, same metric type, overlapping symptomatic populations, independent studies: P-1225's plasma p-tau181 AUC of 0.910 lies above P-1231's entire P-tau181 range (0.610-0.840), and P-1225's sensitivity of 86.36% (95% CI 77.29-95.34) excludes P-1231's sensitivity range (67-71%). If picking out A+T+ patients inside a symptomatic clinic sample is at least as hard as separating AD and aMCI patients from controls, an AUC above the literature's range contradicts it. (b) A claim-level conflict: P-1231 finds blood P-tau181 rising with clinical stage (AD vs aMCI ratio of means 1.36, 1.20-1.54, p < 0.001), while P-1225 concludes that plasma p-tau181 was 'not influenced by the stage or the severity of cognitive decline' and detected no difference between MCI and AD dementia. (c) A ratio-of-means route: P-1225's MCI vs SCD ratio (2.91/2.15 = 1.35; delta-method 95% CI about 1.09-1.68, my computation) against P-1231's aMCI-vs-controls P-tau181 ratio, which the abstract's range (1.36-2.16) suggests could be as high as 2.16.
challenge.why_it_does_or_does_not_succeed: None of the three survives the source documents. (a) The two AUCs have different target conditions and comparators. P-1225 separates A+T+ patients from other patients within SCD and MCI, with AD dementia excluded, no healthy controls, and T defined by CSF p-tau181 (the index analyte, measured in another fluid). P-1231's range is for AD and aMCI patients against controls. P-1231's figure is a range of study-level results from a 32-study systematic review, not a pooled estimate with an interval, so one further study outside it contradicts nothing. P-1225's own AUC has an approximate 95% interval of 0.82-1.00 from its counts (Hanley-McNeil; the first reader's computation, which I reproduced), which reaches below the top of the range. Neither paper establishes that the biomarker-defined problem is the harder one, and P-1225's authors attribute their higher AUC to the A/T(N) target; its sensitivity is taken at a Youden cut-off chosen in the same sample for that different target. (b) On the one quantity both papers actually measure, the unadjusted ratio of plasma p-tau181 concentration in AD dementia to MCI, they agree. P-1225's means (4.03 vs 2.91 pg/mL) give 1.38 (delta-method 1.08-1.77, my computation) against P-1231's pooled 1.36 (1.20-1.54). P-1225's 'no differences ... between MCI and AD demented patients' is a Bonferroni post-hoc non-significance with 14 and 32 patients, so the difference is one of significance only. Its 'not influenced by the stage' is a different estimand, the stage effect adjusted for AP status, and even there its own coefficient is positive with a 95% CI excluding zero (Diagnosis B = 0.415, 0.051-0.778, p = 0.026). The paper calls that coefficient non-significant only against its 0.0125 threshold. The AD dementia vs SCD ratio (1.87, 1.49-2.36, my computation) also falls inside P-1231's AD vs controls 2.06 (1.39-3.06), although SCD is not a control group. (c) P-1231's text prints no aMCI-vs-controls ratio for P-tau181; it appears only in Fig. 4, which is not in the extract, and the abstract's upper value 2.16 matches no printed P-tau181 comparison. P-1225 has no healthy controls: its SCD patients (30.76% AP+ in Table 2) are not 'cognitively healthy volunteers', and it does not restrict its MCI group to amnestic MCI. The population behind the label differs, which is incommensurability. Gates: task (T1 vs T6), dataset family and validation tier fail with no waiver on record. A C-227-style waiver of the task and design gates for a synthesis set against a primary study would be conceivable only if the quantity were shared. An argument for false_positive exists: the record is itself a filed incommensurability note, and the only shared quantity agrees. It does not displace documented_incommensurability, because the contested AUCs are different quantities. The C-238 precedent, where the contested quantities differed and the one shared quantity agreed, was accepted at G4 as documented incommensurability, as was C-239, a record of the same kind. The first reader's grounds stand; (b) adds a ground they did not name, and it points the same way.
grounds: The two AUCs have different target conditions and comparators: A+T+ against other patients inside SCD and MCI with no healthy controls (P-1225), against AD and aMCI patients versus controls (P-1231).
P-1225's reference standard defines T status by CSF p-tau181, the index analyte measured in another fluid, and its authors attribute their higher AUC to the A/T(N) target rather than to the marker.
P-1231's P-tau181 AUC figure is a range of study-level results from a 32-study systematic review, with no pooled estimate or interval that a single study could contradict.

On the one quantity both papers measure, the plasma p-tau181 concentration ratio of AD dementia to MCI, the results agree (P-1225 4.03/2.91 = 1.38; P-1231 pooled 1.36, 1.20-1.54), and P-1225's non-significant post-hoc difference is a difference of significance only.

P-1225's claim that p-tau181 is not influenced by stage is a pathology-adjusted estimand on which its own stage coefficient is positive with a CI excluding zero (B = 0.415, 0.051-0.778), so it does not oppose P-1231's stage gradient.
No ratio-of-means comparison of MCI against controls is available: P-1231 prints no aMCI-vs-controls P-tau181 ratio in its text, and P-1225 has no healthy control group.
The task, dataset-family and validation-tier gates fail with no waiver on record.

conflicts.claim_a: The high-discrimination arm and the weaker evidence. A Framingham-style 0-53 point sociodemographic/self-report score developed in CHARLS and applied to CLHLS and RuLAS, reporting a 5-year ROC-AUC of 0.823 in RuLAS. It is flagged authors_overclaim and its own digest records that its three cohorts do not measure the same outcome, so it supplies the number that must be quarantined, not the number that must be believed.
conflicts.claim_b: The reference arm on outcome ascertainment. BABRI Beijing community cohort, incident MCI adjudicated by Petersen consensus criteria with a five-domain neuropsychological battery; non-cognitive risk-score models reach AUC 0.64-0.70 and only rise to 0.785 once baseline memory and language performance are added. It is not overclaim-flagged and supplies the clinically adjudicated benchmark against which P-824's figure is shown to be measuring something else.
conflicts.conflict_statement: DOCUMENTED INCOMMENSURABILITY, NOT A GENUINE CONFLICT. The corpus's two Chinese community-cohort incident-MCI risk scores appear to disagree by 12 to 18 AUC points about how much non-imaging, non-biomarker survey and history variables predict incident MCI in older Chinese adults - P-824's 0-53 point sociodemographic composite reports a 5-year ROC-AUC of 0.823 in its RuLAS validation cohort, while P-981's non-cognitive risk-score models (RS1/RS2: age, education, cerebrovascular disease, intelligence, physical activities) reach only AUC 0.64-0.70 for ~3-year incident MCI in the BABRI Beijing cohort. The two numbers are not comparable and the apparent superiority of the weaker predictor set is an artefact of the outcome rule: P-824's two validation cohorts define 'incident MCI' by dementia-range screening cut-offs (CMMSE < 18; HDS < 21.5) whereas P-981 adjudicates MCI by Petersen consensus criteria with a five-domain neuropsychological battery. The record's operational content is a gating rule: any future conflict, consensus or ranking record spanning Chinese-cohort MCI-incidence models must gate on the printed outcome rule, not on the label 'incident MCI', and P-824's 0.823 must not be pooled with, or ranked against, discrimination figures computed against clinically adjudicated MCI.

readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_a: Discrimination (ROC AUC) of 5-year incident 'MCI' defined by a single global cognitive screening threshold at follow-up (RuLAS: HDS < 21.5), in community-dwelling adults aged 70-87 in Rugao, by a test-free sociodemographic/self-report score developed in another cohort (external validation).
readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_b: The figures the record cites (0.64-0.70) are apparent ROC AUCs for PREVALENT consensus Petersen (memory-only) MCI versus normal cognition at baseline, in Beijing community adults aged 50-80 with MMSE > 23, from logistic demographic/lifestyle/vascular scores (RS2 includes MMSE). P-981's one incident-MCI estimate (RS3, 0.785) adds memory and fluency test scores and covers a mean follow-up of about 2 to 3 years.
grounds: P-981's 0.640 and 0.712 discriminate prevalent MCI in the baseline cross-section, not incident MCI, so they measure a different quantity from P-824's 5-year incident AUC [q8, q9, q10].

The outcome constructs differ: P-824's validation cohorts count 'MCI' when a global screening score falls below a cut-off (CMMSE < 18, HDS < 21.5, the HDS cut-off sourced from a dementia-screening validation study), whereas P-981 requires a two-expert consensus on Petersen criteria with memory-only impairment [q2, q3, q4, q5, q6, q7].

P-981's one incident-MCI estimate (0.785) comes from a model that adds memory and fluency tests to RS2, which already contains MMSE, a different predictor set from P-824's test-free score [q11, q12, q13].

The horizons differ (5-year AUC in P-824; mean follow-up of about 2 to 3 years in P-981's incident sub-cohort), and the dataset-family and validation-tier gates fail with no waiver on record [q1, q14].
Neither paper claims what the other refutes: both conclude that risk scores built from such factors predict MCI [q1, q15].

record_defects: claim_b and conflict_statement present RS1/RS2 (0.64-0.70) as discrimination of '~3-year incident MCI'; P-981 computes them on prevalent MCI in the 5,921-person baseline cross-section (1,174 MCI vs 4,747 NC; the Figure 1A intervals of about +/-0.02 fit that sample, not 72 incident events). Only RS3 (0.785) is an incident-MCI model [q8, q9, q10].
RS1/RS2 are called 'non-cognitive'; RS2 includes MMSE (MMSE <= 27 carries 6 points in Table 2), and its AUC is 0.712, above the 0.64-0.70 range the record takes from the abstract [q10, q11].

The RS1/RS2 predictor list ('age, education, cerebrovascular disease, intelligence, physical activities') omits sex and income level, which are in Table 2; 'intelligence' is the abstract's word for intellectual activities.
'incident MCI 7.8% (72/849)': 72 of 921 participants normal at baseline developed MCI (7.8%); 849 is the number who stayed normal (the abstract's 'of 849' is the paper's own slip) [q16].
'~3 years': the abstract says 'average 3-year follow-up', but Table 4 gives mean follow-up of 2.25 y for converters and 2.01 y for non-converters.

The evidence quotes attributed to P-824 ('The three cohorts do not measure the same outcome, so the validation is not validation.'; 'The higher of the two external-cohort discrimination figures...'; 'No confidence interval or standard error for any of the paper's three AUCs.') and to P-981 ('RS models 1/2 achieved AUCs between 0.64 and 0.70 (...)'; 'Petersen-criteria consensus MCI diagnoses with five-domain neuropsychological battery.'; 'incident MCI 7.8% (72/849) over ~3 years.') are summary-block wording, not text of the PDFs. The 'no CI' statement is true of P-824's text only, since Figure 1 is not in the extract.

'dementia-range screening cut-offs' is the record's characterisation, not the paper's: P-824 calls CMMSE < 18 and HDS < 21.5 MCI definitions; only its cited sources (a dementia-subtype prevalence study for the CMMSE cut-off and a dementia-screening validation of the HDS) indicate dementia-screening provenance [q3, q4, q5].
Registry row, not ledger text: P-824 prediction_horizon_years is 'not reported', but the paper reports 5-year AUCs and states that 3- and 7-year results were similar (Supplementary Figures 3 and 4).

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: For predicting incident MCI in cognitively normal Chinese community adults, P-824's self-report risk score reached an AUC of 0.870 at 3 years (0.861 at 5 years) in its CHARLS development cohort, against 0.785 for P-981's model with cognitive tests on 72 converters and 849 stable participants (z = 2.3-2.6; neither paper prints an interval). P-824's own external cohorts, however, agree with P-981 within uncertainty (RuLAS 0.831 and CLHLS 0.794 at 3 years), so the discrepancy rests on the two development-cohort estimates. The outcome label, education acting as both predictor and label determinant, the predictor sets, cohort age and event count are candidate explanations, none shown to be sufficient.
candidate_explanations: Outcome label: CHARLS counts a follow-up cognitive score more than 1 SD below the mean, with no education adjustment. P-981 requires a two-expert Petersen consensus, with memory impairment defined after normative correction for age and education.
Label-predictor overlap: education is P-824's strongest predictor (HR 0.31), and it also shifts an unadjusted score threshold.
Predictors: P-824 uses self-reported factors only; RS3 adds memory and verbal-fluency tests to RS2, which contains MMSE.
Horizon: fixed 3- and 5-year AUCs against about 2-3 years of observed follow-up. P-824's 3-year figure is higher, which argues against horizon as the explanation.
Events: RS3 rests on 72 converters, against 2,323 events in CHARLS.
Cohort and age: CHARLS adults aged 45 and over (mean 57.9) against BABRI adults aged 50-80 with MMSE above 23.
None is shown to be sufficient.

If _metric_parse already refuses slash-separated or parenthetically-qualified Best_Metric strings, or already prefers the last numeric token, this pair never generates and the record documents a hazard that does not exist - reducing it to a bookkeeping entry. A second, sharper objection: the corrective statement 'the two models are concordant' is itself a loose comparison, not a demonstrated equivalence. P-13's 0.844 comes from N=718 over an 8-year horizon; P-1128's 0.880 comes from a 50-subject internal split with no stated horizon and no external cohort. Those two numbers are not commensurable enough to support 'concordant' either - the honest verdict is that this pair supports NO ordering claim in either direction, and a reviewer would be right to make me weaken 'concordant' to 'no ordering is estimable'.

readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_a: P-13: concordance index for time to MCI-to-AD conversion (visits to 96 months) in the ADNI high-risk MCI subgroup defined post hoc by clustering longitudinal FAQ trajectories, for a dynamic Cox model on longitudinal CDRSB and hippocampal-volume trajectory scores plus baseline cognition, demographics and APOE e4; the headline 0.844 is the apparent (training) estimate.
readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_b: P-1128: concordance index for time to MCI-to-AD conversion within 60 months in ADNI MCI selected as converters within 60 months or patients stable for 5 years (reverters excluded), for a baseline Cox model on T1 cortical morphology and gray-matter network radiomics plus MoCA and FAQ; 0.880 on a 50-patient random hold-out (0.951 in training).
grounds: P-13's 0.844 is the training-set C-index of a high-risk-subgroup model (237 training patients of 340 high-risk of 718), with 0.829 after optimism correction and 0.805 on its test split, so it is neither the population nor the evaluation level of P-1128's 0.880 [q1, q2, q3].

P-13's subgroup is defined by clustering follow-up FAQ trajectories, a different population behind the label 'MCI' from P-1128's converters within 60 months and 5-year-stable patients with reverters excluded [q4, q8, q9].

The predictor sets and input representations differ: longitudinal CDRSB and hippocampal trajectory scores with baseline cognition and genetic variables in P-13, baseline cortical morphology and network radiomics with MoCA and FAQ in P-1128 [q5, q6, q11].

challenge.by: second model reader instructed to argue the verdict into a genuine contradiction (or out of one), reading both source documents in full
challenge.strongest_case_against_the_verdict: Take the quantity as Harrell's C-index for time to MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI MCI from a structural-MRI-plus-clinical Cox model under internal random-split validation. On the PDFs all four review gates then match: both are T2; both use ADNI; both have a random held-out split (P-13 237/103, P-1128 112/50), which is V3 by the extraction template's own definition, so P-13's registry V2 is a miscoding; and both combine structural MRI with clinical scales. The metric type is identical, and like for like the results are far apart: training 0.951 (0.928-0.974) against 0.844 (0.815-0.873), with non-overlapping intervals, and hold-out 0.880 (0.817-0.943), whose interval excludes P-13's 0.805. There is also an ordering angle: P-13 states that 'All the longitudinal models performed better than the baseline models' and that hippocampal volume is 'the best predictive marker for AD', while P-1128's baseline whole-cortex radiomics model beats P-13's longitudinal hippocampus-plus-CDRSB model, and P-1128 claims 'higher accuracy' than hippocampus-focused models. Shared ADNI participants make the comparison tighter, not looser.
challenge.why_it_does_or_does_not_succeed: It does not succeed, and the reason is the rule's definition of a contradiction, not the gate. (1) The two C-indices belong to two different models with different predictor sets and input representations. The rule lists different methods each reporting a different score, with no refuted ordering claim, as not incompatible. The interval around an apparent C-index describes the sampling variability of that fitted model on that sample, not a population parameter both papers estimate. (2) The estimand differs in population and horizon. P-13's C-index is confined to a high-risk subgroup chosen by clustering follow-up FAQ trajectories, with longitudinal inputs over visits to 96 months. P-1128 keeps only converters within 60 months and 5-year-stable patients, and excludes reverters. P-13 itself shows the size of this effect: baseline ADAS13 scores 0.677 in its high-risk group and 0.825 in its low-risk group, a spread about twice the 0.075 hold-out gap. (3) The ordering angle fails. P-13's longitudinal-over-baseline result compares versions of the same markers inside its own subgroup, and P-1128 tests no longitudinal model (it names 'did not analyze dynamic follow-up data' as a limitation). The hippocampus sentence is P-13 citing Teipel et al. 2013, not its own finding. P-1128's superiority claim is made against its refs 7 and 9, its 37 features include left-hippocampus network features, and P-13's lower figures agree with P-1128's claim rather than refute it. (4) The C-80, C-204 and C-232 precedents each had a stronger case (C-232's within-study rankings did reverse). They were reclassified as documented incommensurability on input representation, on endpoint and evaluation, and on predictor set and horizon respectively; C-262 fails on the same axes and has no ordering claim at all. (5) On the caller's question: a performance difference between two different models on overlapping ADNI data can be a genuine contradiction under the rule only in two cases. Either the same model or marker set is evaluated for the same estimand with mutually exclusive uncertainty, or one study's own head-to-head ordering is reversed by the other's on a comparable estimand. Neither holds here, and shared participants are recorded as non-independence, not as a route to contradiction. (6) The false_positive direction was also tested, since the record is a filed 'EXAMINED NON-CONFLICT' with paper_b null. Read against the documents, a gap larger than the record states survives and fails on quantity, so documented_incommensurability is the precise outcome. That matches the first reader's filed notes C-253 and C-260 and the closed precedents C-238 and C-239.
grounds: Like for like, P-1128 is higher at both evaluation levels (training 0.951, 0.928-0.974, against 0.844, 0.815-0.873; hold-out 0.880, 0.817-0.943, against 0.805), but these are C-indices of two different models, and the rule counts 'two different methods each reporting a different score where neither study claims the ordering the other refutes' as not incompatible [f2, f11].

The predictor sets and input representations differ: functional principal-component scores of longitudinal CDRSB and hippocampal volume with baseline cognition, demographics and APOE e4 in P-13, against 37 baseline cortical-morphology and gray-matter-network features with MoCA and FAQ in P-1128 [f5, f14; first reader q5].

The populations and horizons differ: P-13's estimate is confined to a high-risk subgroup chosen by clustering FAQ trajectories over visits to 96 months, whereas P-1128 keeps only converters within 60 months and patients stable for 5 years and drops reverters [f1, f4, f10, f12, f13].

P-13 itself shows how far the subgroup moves a C-index: the same baseline predictor (ADAS13) scores 0.677 in its high-risk group and 0.825 in its low-risk group (0.665 and 0.793 after optimism correction), a spread about twice the 0.075 hold-out gap between the papers [f6, f7].

No ordering claim is refuted: P-13's 'longitudinal beats baseline' is a within-subgroup result for the same markers that P-1128 never tests, P-13's hippocampus sentence cites Teipel et al. 2013 rather than its own data, and P-1128's claim of higher accuracy than hippocampus-focused models agrees with P-13's lower figures [f8, f9, f15, f16, f18].

On the PDFs the four deterministic gates can be read as matched (T2; ADNI; a random held-out split in both, V3 by the extraction template's definition, so P-13's registry V2 is a miscoding; structural MRI with clinical scales), so the gate does not block this pair; it fails the same-quantity and incompatibility tests that apply after the gates [f3, f17].

The precedents agree: C-80 (input representation), C-204 (endpoint and evaluation, no ranking contradiction) and C-232 (predictor set and horizon, although its within-study rankings did reverse) were reclassified as documented incommensurability, and C-262 is weaker than each because it contains no ordering claim.

On the caller's question: under the rule as written, a performance gap between two different models on overlapping ADNI data can be genuine only if the same model or marker set is evaluated for the same estimand with mutually exclusive uncertainty, or if one study's own head-to-head ordering is reversed by the other's on a comparable estimand; neither holds here.

It is not a false_positive although the record is a filed note with paper_b null: read against the documents, a like-for-like gap larger than the record states survives (non-overlapping training intervals) and fails on quantity, which is how the first reader treated the filed notes C-253 and C-260 and how C-238 and C-239 were closed.

conflicts.claim_b: Two-phase observational practice survey of 121 neurologists at 17 self-selected Italian memory/neurology centres plus 203 recorded patient decisions; reports BETWEEN-clinician variability in diagnostic criteria, investigations and therapy. It measures dispersion of practice, not who performs the diagnosis, and it publishes no numeric estimate of that dispersion.
conflicts.conflict_statement: DOCUMENTED INCOMMENSURABILITY - explicitly NOT proposed as a genuine conflict. P-1017 (US psychiatrists) and P-1080 (Italian neurologists) pass all four deterministic comparability gates (Task_Type T6, cross_sectional, population_specificity general, modality_subtype survey_questionnaire, both V2) and read as opposite verdicts on whether specialist MCI practice is adequate - 67% of MCI/mild-AD patients personally diagnosed with mental status testing used by 94% and advanced formal MCI/AD training held by 82%, versus 'suboptimal and inconsistent MCI management in Italy' - but the two papers measure different constructs on different clinician populations under different guideline regimes, and P-1080 reports no percentage, agreement statistic or between-centre test for any of its claims, so no gap magnitude exists and neither arm is admissible as the strong arm. The pair should be blocked at claim level and recorded as incommensurable, not promoted.

conflicts.residual_risk: The strongest argument against this record is that it consumes a candidate slot to say 'no'. If negative pair verdicts do not belong in conflicts.json, the correct home for this finding is a lint rule or a gate note, not a record: the substantive content is 'the four deterministic gates cannot separate role-share surveys from practice-dispersion surveys because both normalise to T6 / cross_sectional / general / survey_questionnaire', which is a checker defect, not a knowledge product. A reviewer who wants only positive records should reject this file and instead open a fix on gatecheck's construct blindness for T6 clinician surveys. A second, weaker objection: an operator could argue the pair is not merely incommensurable but flatly concordant - P-1017's own conclusion is a coordination-gap finding - in which case even the incommensurability framing overstates the tension and the pair deserves no record at all.
conflicts.dedup_note: Checked against every genuine conflict listed in the brief (C-80 P-82 x P-3, C-204 P-41 x P-65, C-227 P-655 x P-653, C-232 P-344 x P-309, C-234 P-832 x P-705) - none involves clinician-practice surveys. Checked against the 12 operator conflict verdicts (C-93, C-116, C-117, C-148, C-158, C-112, C-165, C-63, C-92, C-02, C-80, C-P41-P65) - none involves P-1017 or P-1080, and none records a clinician-survey pair. Neither paper appears anywhere in conflict_pool.md (grep for all nine T16_other ids returns zero hits), so this pair was never pre-screened. Checked against T16_other_existing_gaps.md (0 of 535 corpus gaps match this theme) and against existing_gaps.md: ACTOR-G-017 (four incompatible MCI case operationalisations) and ACTOR-G-033 (non-comparable outcome labels) concern how MCI is defined in STUDIES, not how clinicians practise, and G-NEW-1064-A (diagnosis-to-action gap, cited by P-1080's own digest) is a gap statement, not a pair verdict. Checked against the IA ledger: IA-94 (P-1036) and IA-NEW-1046-01 (P-1046) already assert that routine MCI detection is inadequate; this record does not restate that claim, it blocks the invalid inference that P-1017's 67% contradicts it, since P-1017's denominator is the referred specialist caseload.
fp_codes_cleared: DUPLICATE_PAPER: cleared - gatecheck reports no duplicate_of on either row; different countries, specialties, years (2023 vs 2024), venues (BMC Psychiatry vs Neurological Sciences) and disjoint author lists, and neither digest's related-work section names the other.
DESIGN_MISMATCH: cleared - gatecheck prints pass, both are cross_sectional; neither is longitudinal.

TASK_SUBSTAGE_MISMATCH: not adjudicable - gatecheck prints skip, task_substage is 'not reported' on both sides. Neither paper stages conversion at all, so the code cannot fire, but it also cannot certify comparability.
GAP_BELOW_THRESHOLD: not applicable - there is no shared numeric quantity on which a gap could be above or below any threshold.
PREDICTION_HORIZON_MISMATCH: not applicable - neither paper predicts conversion at any horizon.

METRIC_TYPE_MISMATCH: APPLIES, and is decisive. P-1017's Best_Metric is a prevalence-style percentage of a clinician caseload; P-1080's Best_Metric is the string 'Descriptive: 121 neurologists, 203 patients; non-uniform criteria and strategies (no single performance metric)'. The blocking rule routes this to a claim-level conflict flag only, which is exactly what this record is.

POPULATION_SPECIFICITY: APPLIES in substance though not in the column. Both rows code population_specificity 'general' because that column describes the PATIENT population, but the units of analysis here are clinicians: US psychiatrists on an industry-run opt-in panel versus Italian neurologists at self-selected memory centres in a regime P-1080 itself describes as guideline-absent. The column cannot see this, so the gate passes on a comparability that does not exist.

MODALITY_SUBTYPE_MISMATCH: APPLIES in substance though not in the column. Both normalise to 'survey_questionnaire', but P-1017 is a single anonymous attitude/practice questionnaire while P-1080 is a two-phase instrument whose second phase records real decisions on 203 patients - and the two instruments measure different constructs (role share and tool usage versus between-clinician uniformity).

AUTHORS_OVERCLAIM (schema rule 2): APPLIES to BOTH arms, so no strong arm exists. P-1017's card flags the generalisation of a headline conclusion from an n=50 self-report cell; P-1080's card flags the normative 'suboptimal and inconsistent' verdict drawn from a descriptive survey of self-selected centres with no outcome linkage.

grounds: P-1017 measures who diagnoses and with which self-reported tools in a panel of 50 high-volume US psychiatrists [q1, q2, q3, q4].

The favourable and unfavourable verdicts concern different clinician populations and different constructs, and P-1080 itself excluded psychiatrists, so a claim about one cannot contradict the claim about the other [q5, q12].
Where both surveys ask the same question, use of a brief mental-status screen, they agree (94% versus 93.3%) [q2, q11].

The record's statement that P-1080 reports no percentage is wrong, but the percentages it does report describe Italian neurologists or their patients, not US psychiatrists, so they form no incompatible pair [q10, q11].

evidence_quotes.quote: A total of 301 physicians participated in the survey, 50 of whom were psychiatrists.

Of their patients with all-cause MCI or mild AD dementia, psychiatrists reported personally diagnosing two-thirds (67%). Psychiatrists used various methods to diagnose MCI or mild AD dementia including mental status testing (94%)
HCPs who had previously opted in to participate in online research surveys were recruited via email.
Most respondents reported subspecializing in geriatric psychiatry (70%) or neuropsychiatry (56%).
They can provide timely and accurate diagnosis of clinical MCI and mild AD dementia and develop optimal treatment plans for patients.
Self-reporting is a limitation inherent to survey-based research.

Information gathered in the first phase of the survey highlighted a non-uniform use of diagnostic criteria and procedures for MCI, as well as a very heterogeneous therapeutic strategy among Italian neurologists.
The results of our study reflect a suboptimal management of MCI patients in Italy and highlight the need of standardized diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for this condition.

record_defects: conflict_statement: 'P-1080 reports no percentage, agreement statistic or between-centre test for any of its claims, so no gap magnitude exists': P-1080 prints many percentages (Table 1: MMSE 93.3%, MoCA 57.1%, second-level neuropsychology 70.4%, brain MRI 97.5%; Table 2: MMSE in 95.1% of patients; 83.1% use the MCI category). It reports no agreement statistic or between-centre test, which is right [q10, q11].

claim_b: '17 self-selected Italian memory/neurology centres': the board invited 17 centres 'deliberately chosen' for their MCI activity and all accepted; clinicians were also chosen for experience. The sample is selected, not self-selected (still non-random) [q9, q13].

The P-1017 evidence quote 'Psychiatrists already diagnose and manage most MCI/mild AD patients they see but do not perceive themselves as care coordinators, exposing a coordination gap in the care pathway.' and the inference that P-1017's 'own conclusion is itself a gap finding' are summary-block wording; the paper's conclusion is favourable ('They can provide timely and accurate diagnosis ...') and mentions the coordinator point as a qualification. The incommensurability does not rest on that reading [q5].

Other quotes attributed to the papers ('Opt-in online survey panel; modest psychiatrist cell (n=50); ...'; 'Descriptive: 121 neurologists, 203 patients; ...'; 'Survey-based, descriptive design; self-selected participating centres/neurologists; ...'; 'MCI is clinically heterogeneous ... non-uniform or absent') are summary-block or registry wording, not PDF text; 'About one-third of patients ...' paraphrases the paper's 'Almost one-third of patients suspected of having MCI or mild AD dementia are referred to specialists including psychiatrists.' [q15].
'a US specialty in which 82% of respondents report advanced formal MCI/AD training': the 82% is of the 50 psychiatrists, not of all 301 respondents.

'The Italian setting is a stated guideline-absent regime': P-1080 says there is no unanimously accepted practical guidance, but also refers to 'the proposed Italian guidelines for a biological diagnosis of MCI'; 'guideline-absent' overstates [q14].

'pass all four deterministic comparability gates': those are the gatecheck columns; under the review's four gates the dataset-family gate fails (a US panel versus an Italian centre network), with no waiver on record.

readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_a: Cross-sectional difference in blood NfL concentration between MCI (any subtype, as each included study defined it) and healthy controls, as a standardised mean difference. It rests on three small case-control comparisons published before May 2021, all measured by Simoa (2 plasma, 1 serum).
readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_b: Cross-sectional difference in blood NfL concentration between amnestic MCI and cognitively healthy controls, as a ratio of means. It comes from part of 23 blood-NfL studies searched to May 17, 2021, with assays pooled (the paper names ELISA, IMR and SIMOA).
grounds: On the contested quantity the two syntheses point the same way. P-1341's blood estimates are positive but not significant (plasma SMD 0.10, -0.36 to 0.56; Simoa, i.e. all blood, SMD 0.01, -0.38 to 0.41; p.3, p.4). P-1231's aMCI-vs-control ratio of means is 1.24 (1.17-1.32; p.3).

What differs is statistical significance, which Section 5.2 of the review says is not a data conflict. P-1341 claims no equivalence. It hedges its blood finding ('may be not a biomarker ... more studies on blood NfL are needed') and names its small samples as a limitation (p.5).

The reported uncertainty does not show the two results excluding each other. P-1341's plasma interval reaches a moderate positive SMD of 0.56. On P-1341's own blood-study dispersions (Table 1, p.3), that overlaps the SMD range implied by P-1231's interval of 1.17-1.32 (approximate conversion; see incompatible_if_same).

The record misreads P-1341. It files the pair as 'semantic_directional', but the directions agree. Its proposed ELISA/ECL-vs-Simoa resolution cannot be drawn from P-1341, because there the assay split is the CSF/blood split: the 4 ELISA comparisons are the 4 CSF comparisons, and the 3 Simoa comparisons are the 3 blood comparisons (Table 1, p.3; p.4).

Even had the results disagreed, the two are not one estimand. The metrics differ (SMD vs ratio of means; P-1231 p.2), the case labels differ (MCI of any subtype vs amnestic MCI; P-1231 p.2) and the assays differ (Simoa only vs pooled platforms; P-1231 p.6). That would point to documented incommensurability, not a genuine contradiction. The brief's order of application puts the false-positive finding first.

record_defects: residual_risk says P-1341 searched 'to ~2022'. P-1341 searched for studies published before May 1, 2021 (p.2), so both searches closed in May 2021.

residual_risk says P-1341's 'blood signal was significant with ELISA/ECL but not with Simoa'. P-1341 has no blood ELISA or ECL estimate. Its four ELISA comparisons are its four CSF comparisons, and its three Simoa comparisons are its three blood comparisons (Table 1, p.3). The ELISA estimate is identical to the CSF estimate (SMD 0.61, 0.21-1.01), so assay and matrix are confounded. ECL appears only as a historical method in the Discussion (p.5).
residual_risk calls the blood subgroup underpowered with '7 studies total'. The blood subgroup has three comparisons (two plasma, one serum); seven is the total across CSF and blood (Table 1, p.3).

conflict_statement attaches 'NfL AUC 0.59-0.92' to P-1231's aMCI finding. In P-1231 that range comes from a narrative review of 32 diagnostic-accuracy studies and covers identifying 'AD and aMCI patients from controls' (p.5). It is not an estimate for the aMCI-vs-control contrast.

conflict_type 'semantic_directional' is wrong. P-1341's blood point estimates are positive (plasma SMD 0.10; Simoa SMD 0.01), the same direction as P-1231's ratio of 1.24; the two differ in significance only.

review_note objects that P-1231's per-contrast significance is 'inferred, not stated'. The P-1231 PDF states it: aMCI vs controls 1.24, 95% CI 1.17-1.32, p < 0.001 (p.3). The statement's 'significantly' is supported.

readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_a: Hazard of incident all-cause MCI in CU adults with a first-degree family history of AD, as a Cox HR over a mean 5.65 years after plasma sampling. MCI: blinded consensus requiring more than 1.0 SD below norms on an RBANS composite or two RAVLT scores, plus a subjective memory complaint and/or observed decline. Exposure: joint plasma A+T+ (or A-T+) status vs A-T-, with thresholds anchored to Abeta-PET-negative CU adults.
readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_b: Hazard of the NC-to-MCI transition in a random community sample aged 60+, as a multistate Markov HR on an age time scale over a mean 9.6 years (up to 16). MCI: psychometric, 1.5 SD or more below the age-specific mean in at least one of five domains with preserved function; reversion allowed. Exposure: single serum markers above vs below Youden cut-offs derived for 10-year all-cause dementia (p-tau217 > 0.134 pg/mL; 37% of participants 'high'), plus continuous splines.
grounds: The exposure contrasts differ. P-1403's HR of 7.81 compares joint plasma A+T+ with A-T-, on thresholds anchored to Abeta-PET-negative CU adults; A+T+ is 10% of its sample (p.3, p.4). P-1421's HR of 1.07 compares serum p-tau217 above vs below a cut-off tuned to predict 10-year all-cause dementia, with 803 of 2148 participants 'high' (p.4, p.6). P-1421 has no A/T classification. P-1403 reports no whole-sample single-marker or continuous hazard ratio: its Cox models are by A/T group only, and its continuous analysis is ROC AUC (p.4, p.8).

The population behind the 'cognitively unimpaired older adults' label differs. PREVENT-AD enrols only people with a first-degree family history of AD (p.3). SNAC-K is a random community sample aged 60+ with median age 72.2, 865 of 2148 aged 78 or over (p.2, p.6). Both papers note that MCI can arise without AD pathology: P-1403 says most A-T- progressors probably have non-neurodegenerative conditions (p.10), and P-1421 says mild cognitive deficits are not necessarily the expression of an underlying neuropathology (p.5). P-1403 also names community settings as untested (p.3).
The dataset-family gate fails (PREVENT-AD vs SNAC-K) and no waiver is on the record. Under the C-232 precedent, waiving the cohort gate would not cure an exposure (predictor) mismatch.

The endpoint and horizon differ. P-1403 counts consensus MCI requiring a subjective complaint and/or observed decline, over a mean 5.65 years after plasma (p.4). P-1421 counts psychometric MCI (1.5 SD or more below the age-specific mean in one domain) with reversion modelled, over a mean 9.6 years (p.2, p.6).
Matrix and assay differ: plasma on an in-house Gothenburg Simoa vs serum on the ALZpath Simoa. P-1421 states that its cohort-derived cut-offs may not carry over to other laboratory platforms (p.6).

On the closest shared quantity, amyloid alone, the two agree: both are null (P-1403 p.7; P-1421 Table 2, p.4). Including Abeta42/40 in the record's disagreement therefore adds no disagreement. The tension is confined to the tau arm, where the exposures differ.

In fairness to the candidate: P-1421's null also holds for continuous p-tau217 (splines, p.2), so the tension is not only a cut-off artefact, and the two papers' headline answers do diverge. It stays unadjudicable because no like-for-like hazard ratio exists across the two papers.

papers_read.title_as_printed: Plasma p-tau217 identifies cognitively normal older adults who will develop cognitive impairment in a 10-year window
Blood biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease and progression across different stages of cognitive decline in the community

challenge.by: second model reader instructed to argue the verdict into a genuine contradiction (or out of one), reading both source documents in full
challenge.strongest_case_against_the_verdict: The two papers ask the same question about the same marker in the same kind of person with the same metric: does elevated baseline blood p-tau217 in cognitively unimpaired older adults raise the hazard of incident MCI? P-1403 says yes, in its title. Its effect sits entirely on the tau dimension (A+T+ 7.81, 3.92-15.59; A-T+ 4.25, 1.60-11.31; A+T- 1.14, 0.58-2.24), and the authors state that amyloid did not improve the predictive value of the tau markers, so the joint A/T contrast is in substance a p-tau217 contrast. P-1421 says no, for p-tau217 as a dichotomy (1.07, 0.73-1.56; adjusted 1.19, 0.75-1.88), as a continuous spline and in marker combinations. Both of P-1403's tau-positive intervals exclude P-1421's basic interval, and the A+T+ interval excludes the adjusted one as well. Task (T2, normal cognition to MCI), modality family (blood biomarkers) and validation tier (n/a) match. The dataset-family mismatch is what independent replication looks like and could be waived, as the cohort difference in C-232 was. Cut-point differences are a matter of degree: a continuous null across P-1421's whole range leaves no threshold at which a hazard ratio of 4 to 8 could appear.
challenge.why_it_does_or_does_not_succeed: The case fails because neither paper reports an estimate on a quantity the other reports, and the differences that separate the nearest pair are differences of estimand, not of gate. (1) Continuous p-tau217 is an AUC in P-1403 (plasma p-tau217 alone 0.75, Figure 3B) and a spline HR against the median in P-1421, which reports no AUC. (2) P-1403 never reports T+ vs T-. Its nearest contrast, A-T+ vs A-T-, conditions on normal amyloid and rests on 7 exposed participants, and its separation from P-1421 holds only against the basic model (lower bound 1.60 vs upper bound 1.56); it disappears against the adjusted 0.75-1.88. (3) The cut-points define different contrasts. P-1403's T+ sits 2 SD above the mean of Abeta-PET-negative CU adults (13% of its sample; specificity 97%, sensitivity 34% for progression), chosen 'to optimize the detection of AD pathology'. P-1421's cut is the Youden optimum for 10-year all-cause dementia, with 37% of the sample 'high'. From Table 1's quartiles (Q3 0.12 pg/mL under age 78), fewer than 321 of the 1,283 participants under 78 can be above 0.134 pg/mL, so at least 483 of the 803 'high' participants (60% or more) are aged 78 or over, whereas PREVENT-AD's plasma sample averages 65 years. Neither paper places P-1403's 3.98 pg/mL plasma threshold on P-1421's serum z-axis, so the spline cannot be read at P-1403's threshold; the 'continuous null' argument therefore does not reach P-1403's contrast. (4) The endpoint differs in construct. P-1403's MCI is a consensus diagnosis requiring a complaint and/or decline over multiple annual follow-ups, judged on all time points. P-1421's is a per-visit psychometric state (1.5 SD below the age-specific mean in one domain) with reversion modelled, assessed every six years under age 78; its NC-to-MCI hazard is a reversible transition intensity, and the authors note that such deficits are not necessarily the expression of an underlying neuropathology. (5) P-1403 scopes its claim ('Future studies in diverse populations and community settings are needed'), so a community null answers a question P-1403 left open rather than refuting its result. A dataset-family waiver would be reasonable, and the verdict should not rest on the gate; but a waiver cannot supply a shared exposure scale or a shared endpoint (the C-232/C-80 reasoning). No corpus study bridges the pair on a comparable quantity: P-1346 studies memory-clinic MCI to AD, and P-1289 studies amyloid and MCI due to AD in SCD. I checked all 25 first-reader quotes on their cited pages (all verbatim, four after joining a line-break hyphen) and every number in their file against the PDFs, and found no factual error. Figure 3 now supplies the plasma-specific AUCs that record_defect 2 said the text omits: 0.75 for p-tau217 alone and 0.77 combined with Abeta42/40.
grounds: No shared continuous estimate exists: P-1403 gives continuous plasma p-tau217 only as a ROC AUC (0.75 alone, Figure 3B), and P-1421 gives continuous serum p-tau217 only as spline HRs against its median, so the metric types differ.
No shared dichotomous estimate exists: P-1403's Cox models are by joint A/T group against A-T-, and it reports no T+ vs T- or whole-sample p-tau217 hazard ratio.

The nearest pairing, A-T+ vs A-T- (4.25, 1.60-11.31; 7 vs 127 participants), conditions on normal plasma amyloid, which P-1421's contrast does not, and its interval overlaps P-1421's fully adjusted 0.75-1.88.

The thresholds differ by construction: P-1403's T+ (2 SD above the Abeta-PET-negative mean; 13% positive; 97% specificity) targets AD pathology, while P-1421's cut (Youden for 10-year all-cause dementia; 37% high) targets dementia, and at least 60% of P-1421's high group is aged 78 or over (derived from Table 1 quartiles).

The endpoint differs in construct: P-1403 counts persistent consensus MCI with a complaint and/or observed decline on annual assessments, while P-1421 models a reversible per-visit psychometric state assessed every three or six years.

Horizon and model differ: P-1403 fits a Cox model from plasma sampling over a mean 5.65 years, while P-1421 fits a Gompertz multistate Markov intensity on an age time scale over a mean 9.6 years (up to 16).

The population behind the label differs (family-history-enriched CU adults, mean age 65 and 41% APOE e4, vs a random community sample with median age 72 and 40% aged 78 or over), and P-1403 itself names community settings as untested.
The dataset-family mismatch could reasonably be waived, but a waiver cannot cure the exposure and endpoint differences (C-232 and C-80 reasoning), so the verdict does not depend on the gate.
On amyloid, the only other overlapping arm, both papers are null with overlapping intervals (1.14, 0.58-2.24 vs 0.98, 0.72-1.34), so there is no second site of disagreement.

unresolved_discrepancy_2026_09_30.summary: In cognitively unimpaired older adults, plasma p-tau217 with amyloid positivity carried an HR for incident MCI of 7.81 (95% CI 3.92-15.59) in the family-history-enriched PREVENT-AD cohort (P-1403), against an HR of 1.07 (0.73-1.56) for high vs low serum p-tau217 in the SNAC-K community sample (P-1421). The gap is beyond combined uncertainty (log-scale z = 4.95) and unresolved; population enrichment, an extreme AD-anchored A/T contrast against a dementia-tuned single-marker split, the MCI definition, the model and the assay might explain it but are not shown to.
candidate_explanations: Population: a first-degree family-history research cohort (mean age 65) against a random community sample aged 60+ (865/2148 aged 78+). P-1403: 'individuals with a first-degree family history of AD'.

Exposure contrast and threshold: joint A/T groups with T+ set 2 SD above Abeta-PET-negative adults (13% T+), against a single-marker split at a cut-off tuned for 10-year dementia (0.134 pg/mL; 37% high). P-1403: 'The thresholds were selected to optimize the detection of AD pathology, not to detect MCI with no AD pathology.'
P-1403's tau cut-off is 97% specific but 34% sensitive for incident MCI, so the T+ group is small and extreme.
Age confounding of P-1421's dichotomy: 'AD blood biomarker levels increase with age ... suggests the potential need for age-adjusted cutoffs.'
MCI definition: consensus 1.0 SD plus a complaint or observed decline, against psychometric 1.5 SD with reversion modelled.
Model: multistate Markov model on an age time scale with death absorbing and NC-to-dementia forced through MCI, against a Cox model on time since plasma sampling.
Matrix and assay: plasma on an in-house Gothenburg Simoa against serum on the ALZpath Simoa; P-1421 says its cut-offs 'may not fully extend to ... alternative laboratory platforms'.
Selection in P-1421: participants without biomarkers were older and sicker, and their 'exclusion may have led to an underestimation of the results'.
Small groups in P-1403 (21 A+T+, 7 A-T+; mean 5.65 years) against 803/1345 over 9.6 years; 'the HRs between groups should be interpreted with caution'.
Neither paper shows any of these to be sufficient.

conflicts.blocker_flag_operator_review_2026_09_14: WHICH BLOCKER IS HARDER. review_note already records three: (i) population - P-1407's cohort is Lewy-body enriched (62 probable MCI-LB of 131 with outcome data) with an MCI-AD arm of only n=43; (ii) estimand - P-1407's endpoint is a composite 'dementia OR death' while P-1267's is adjudicated dementia conversion only, censored at M36, and the candidate 'acknowledges this but still asserts estimand_match'; (iii) asymmetry - P-1407 reports only a null ('A-beta42/40 was not prognostic in any group') with no HR, CI or p-value, against P-1267's HR 0.36 (95% CI 0.15-0.87). FLAG: the ESTIMAND mismatch, not the population coding, is the harder blocker, and it CANNOT be fixed by re-coding population_specificity. Re-coding population is a registry edit that would make the pair look more comparable to the deterministic gates while leaving the two papers measuring different quantities - a composite endpoint that absorbs deaths versus an adjudicated conversion endpoint that censors them - so the pair would become MORE likely to survive to a gate, not less, without the incomparability being resolved. Combined with blocker (iii), there is no HR from P-1407 that could be placed against P-1267's HR 0.36 even if the estimands were aligned. Flagged only; no re-coding requested, no field altered.

readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_a: Hazard of the composite endpoint dementia-or-death, time to event with no fixed horizon (median time to event 2.0 years; mean follow-up about 3 years). Per control-referenced SD of the inverted plasma Abeta42/40 ratio (Simoa, total peptide). Population: Newcastle MCI cohort aged 60 or over, about half probable MCI-LB (62 of 120 in the whole-cohort model) plus a possible MCI-LB group; MCI-AD (n = 43) and MCI-LB subgroups assigned from the final diagnosis after follow-up. Covariates: age, sex, education, MMSE.
readjudication_2026_09_27.quantity_b: Hazard of adjudicated conversion to dementia (96% probable AD), censored at 36 months. Per percentage point of plasma Abeta1-42/Abeta1-40, and for the highest quartile vs the three lower quartiles, on INNO-BIA free and total fractions. Population: BALTAZAR memory-clinic MCI with Lewy body, parkinsonian, frontotemporal and vascular MCI excluded. Covariates: age, sex, education, APOE e4.
grounds: P-1407 does report Abeta42/40 hazard ratios with 95% intervals in every group (Table 1, p.3). The record's 'not prognostic' is a set of non-significant estimates, not an absence of data.

Two of the three P-1407 estimates point the same way as P-1267's protective high ratio: whole cohort 1.06 and probable MCI-LB 1.23, with the ratio inverted so higher means more abnormal. P-1267 gives continuous HRs of 0.95 per point (free) and 0.92 (total), and top-quartile HRs of 0.36 and 0.37.

The one opposite point estimate, MCI-AD 0.67 (0.37-1.20, p = 0.180), is not supported by P-1407's own statistics. The authors attribute their MCI-AD nulls to 43 cases and 21 events. So there are no 'opposite directions each supported by the study's own statistics'.

No reported interval excludes the other, because the two contrasts sit on scales the printed figures cannot reconcile. What remains is a difference in significance, which Section 5.2 says is not a data conflict; as the operator wrote for C-234, the difference is one of precision, not direction.

P-1267's positive result is itself conditional on adjustment and on grouping the lower quartiles after inspection: unadjusted free top-quartile HR 0.43 (0.18-1.03), p = 0.058; free continuous 0.97, p = 0.21; adjusted global quartile test p = 0.13.

Had the results disagreed, the pair would still be documented incommensurability, not genuine: (a) endpoint, dementia-or-death vs dementia censored at 36 months; (b) population, Lewy body MCI excluded in P-1267 but about half of P-1407's whole cohort; (c) contrast and assay, per control-SD Simoa vs per-point and top-quartile INNO-BIA; (d) the dataset-family gate fails with no waiver on record.
